The Atacama Desert is a plateau in South America, located mostly in northern Chile and reaching in places toward southern Peru. It is usually described as the driest non-polar desert in the world, and some weather stations in its interior have recorded no significant rainfall for years. The desert lies between the Pacific Ocean to the west and the Andes Mountains to the east, forming a narrow north-south strip along the coast.

It covers roughly 105,000 square kilometres (about 41,000 sq mi), though broader definitions include the surrounding arid lands. Its extreme dryness comes from a combination of factors. The cold Humboldt Current offshore suppresses evaporation and cloud formation, the subtropical high-pressure system inhibits precipitation, and the Andes block moist air from the Amazon Basin. Most of the region receives only a few millimetres of rain a year, and some central areas may go decades without measurable precipitation.

Vegetation is sparse in the hyper-arid core, but cacti, shrubs, and hardy grasses grow in less extreme zones. Coastal fog, known locally as camanchaca, provides moisture for some ecosystems. Insects, reptiles, birds, and mammals adapted to aridity live there, and the high-altitude wetlands and salt flats support flamingos and other Andean species.

Indigenous peoples have long lived in the desert, including the Atacameño, or Likan Antai, who built settlements in oases and river valleys. Spain took control of the region during European colonization, and in the 19th century its deposits of nitrates, copper, and other minerals made it economically important. Disputes over these resources contributed to the War of the Pacific (1879-1884), after which Chile gained extensive desert territory formerly held by Peru and Bolivia.

Mining is still a major industry there, especially for copper and lithium. The desert is also important for astronomy. Its high elevation, minimal cloud cover, low humidity, and low light pollution make it one of the best places on Earth to observe the sky. Observatories in or near the region include the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) and several facilities on Cerro Paranal and La Silla.

Tourists and researchers visit as well. The landscape includes salt flats, volcanoes, geysers, and eroded rock formations. Because its dry conditions resemble those of Mars, the desert has been used as an analogue environment for testing space exploration technology and studying the limits of life.

drafts:
Moving to a new city feels, at first, like living someone else's life, someone braver than me. The decision usually starts out vague: a job offer, a school, a relationship, a wish to start over. On paper the move looks tidy. In practice it is cardboard boxes, forwarded mail, a GPS reading out directions in a robot voice, and waking up in a room where the light falls differently on the wall. What you gain and what you give up arrive together, and they are hard to pull apart.

The best thing about a new city is that it lets you start over as a person. Where you have always lived, repetition settles who you are. You are someone's child, someone's friend, the person who orders the usual at the coffee shop or skips certain streets because of old memories. Here, nobody knows those stories unless you tell them. That can be lonely. It can also be a relief, because you can be more social or more private, try new routines and new neighborhoods, even a different personality. Nobody in a new city asks who you used to be, so you get to decide how you move through it.

Discovery is the other pleasure. Buying groceries becomes a small expedition. You notice the architecture, the slang, the weather, how people wait in line or greet strangers. You find out where the best bread is, which park is quietest at dusk, which train platform fills up fastest in the rain. The details pile up slowly, and the place stops being a map and starts being home. Daily life turns out not to be fixed, and it can still surprise you.

The costs are real, though, and harder to add up than rent and a moving truck. Homesickness is the obvious one, but the word sounds too soft for what it can be. You miss people, and you also miss the version of yourself that existed without effort around them. In the old city you knew how to belong. In the new one, belonging is work. You have to find a doctor, a mechanic, a favorite café, someone to call when something breaks. Even small errands wear you out when there is no cushion of familiarity under them.

Distance makes love less convenient. Friendships that proximity used to carry have to survive on texts, planned calls, and expensive visits. Family milestones happen without you, or you go back and find that home kept changing while you were gone. The city you left does not wait for you, preserved. It moves on, the way you do, and there is grief in seeing that.

Maybe a life only gets bigger by being unsettled first. The new city gives you freedom, novelty, and growth, and it charges you in uncertainty, loneliness, and loss. Moving means agreeing to that trade. If you are lucky, the strange streets eventually become your streets, and the costs, which never disappear, begin to feel less like penalties.

**Hospital network reports data breach that may affect thousands of patients**

A large regional hospital network said Tuesday that it is investigating a data breach that may have exposed the personal and medical information of thousands of patients.

The network operates several hospitals, outpatient clinics, and specialty care centers across the region. It detected suspicious activity in its computer systems earlier this month. Officials said in a statement that the organization moved quickly to contain the incident, started an internal investigation, and hired outside cybersecurity experts to determine how far the breach reached.

Preliminary findings suggest unauthorized actors may have accessed patient records containing names, dates of birth, addresses, phone numbers, medical record numbers, insurance details, and, in some cases, limited clinical information. Officials said there is no evidence so far that financial account or payment card data was compromised. The investigation is continuing.

"We take the privacy and security of our patients' information extremely seriously," the hospital network said in its statement. "Upon discovering this issue, we immediately implemented containment measures, notified law enforcement, and began working with leading forensic specialists to assess what information may have been affected."

The network did not say how many patients are involved but called the breach "significant." It expects to notify affected patients by mail in the coming weeks and will offer eligible patients free credit monitoring and identity protection services as a precaution.

Hospital operations have continued. Some administrative systems were taken offline temporarily, which delayed scheduling and access to certain online services. Emergency departments and inpatient care were not disrupted, according to officials.

Cybersecurity experts say healthcare organizations remain attractive targets for hackers because they hold so much sensitive personal and medical data. Unlike a stolen credit card number, a medical record can contain permanent identifying details that can be used for identity theft, insurance fraud, or phishing attacks.

"This type of incident can have long-lasting consequences for patients," said one data privacy analyst not affiliated with the hospital network. "Even if clinical care is unaffected, the loss of trust can be substantial, especially when health information is involved."

Federal health privacy rules, including the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, or HIPAA, require covered entities to safeguard patient information and to notify individuals when certain breaches occur. Regulators are likely to review the breach under those rules.

Patients are being advised to watch for unexpected bills, insurance statements, or suspicious emails and phone calls that mention their medical care. The network said it is strengthening system security, reviewing access controls, and taking additional steps to prevent similar incidents.

Knowing a subject well is not enough to make someone a good teacher. A teacher also needs patience, passion, empathy, and a way of making students feel seen. I think the best ones build a room where learning seems possible.

Patience comes first for me. Students learn at different speeds, and a teacher who gets frustrated when one of them struggles has already lost that student. A patient teacher tries another explanation, then another example. That tells a student who doubts themselves that difficulty is not failure and that understanding can take a while. It also teaches perseverance.

Passion matters because students can tell whether a teacher cares about the material. Someone who talks about literature or mathematics with real interest can bring a hard topic to life, and a list of facts becomes something worth remembering. Students also see that learning can be a pleasure rather than a chore.

A good teacher remembers being confused, nervous, or afraid of making mistakes, and knows that students bring unseen weight into the room: trouble at home, stress, loneliness, pressure to succeed. So they listen, and they notice the student who has gone quiet. Sometimes encouragement at the right moment does more than an explanation. A student who feels understood will speak up, take risks, and believe improvement is possible.

Kindness does not mean lower standards. Some of the most effective teachers expect a great deal because they can see what their students might do. They push students to think harder and aim higher than they would on their own, and they back those expectations with support. They help students get there.

Years later, students forget dates and formulas, but they remember how a teacher made them feel. They remember the one who believed in them when they were unsure, who sparked an interest they had never considered, or who showed them that their voice mattered. Good teachers shape character as well as knowledge, and they help students learn about themselves along with the world.

# Commit message style guide

A good commit message helps teammates review a change and helps future maintainers understand why it was made. It also makes debugging with `git log` and `git blame` easier. Follow these conventions for every commit.

## Structure

```
<subject line>

<body>

<footer>
```

Separate the subject from the body with a blank line. The body and footer are optional for trivial changes.

## Subject line

- **Limit to 50 characters.** The hard limit is 72.

# Tbilisi

**Tbilisi** (Georgian: თბილისი), historically known as **Tiflis**, is the capital and largest city of Georgia. It lies on the banks of the Mtkvari (Kura) River and had a population of approximately 1.2 million in the early 2020s, roughly a third of the country's inhabitants. The city is a cultural, economic, and transportation hub in the South Caucasus.

## History

According to tradition, King Vakhtang I Gorgasali of Iberia founded the city in the 5th century AD after discovering warm sulfur springs while hunting. The name derives from the Old Georgian *tbili*, meaning "warm." His successors moved the royal seat to Tbilisi, and the city grew in importance despite repeated invasions by Persians, Byzantines, Arabs, Mongols, and Turkic dynasties.

Tbilisi flourished during the Georgian Golden Age under King David IV and Queen Tamar in the 12th and early 13th centuries, although it was later sacked several times, notably by Timur and by the Persian ruler Agha Mohammad Khan in 1795. Georgia was annexed by the Russian Empire in the early 19th century, and Tbilisi became the administrative center of the Caucasus Viceroyalty. After a brief independence from 1918 to 1921, the city became the capital of the Georgian Soviet Socialist Republic. Georgia regained independence in 1991, and Tbilisi has since seen political upheaval, including the Rose Revolution of 2003, as well as modernization.

## Geography and climate

The city occupies a valley surrounded by mountains and hills, at an elevation of roughly 400–770 meters above sea level. Tbilisi has a transitional climate between humid subtropical and continental, with hot summers and cool winters.

## Culture and architecture

Tbilisi's architecture is eclectic, mixing medieval, neoclassical, Art Nouveau, Soviet, and contemporary styles. The Old Town (Dzveli Tbilisi) has narrow streets, carved wooden balconies, and the sulfur baths of Abanotubani. Landmarks include the Narikala Fortress, the Metekhi Church, the Sioni Cathedral, the Holy Trinity Cathedral (Sameba), and the modern Bridge of Peace. The Kartlis Deda ("Mother of Georgia") statue overlooks the city from Sololaki Ridge.

The city has theaters, museums, and festivals, including the Georgian National Museum and the Rustaveli Theatre. Georgian cuisine, including *khachapuri*, *khinkali*, and local wines, is part of the city's identity. Its nightlife and electronic music scene are also known internationally.

## Economy and transport

Tbilisi is the country's financial and commercial center, with major sectors including services, tourism, trade, and manufacturing. The Tbilisi Metro, opened in 1966, is the city's main rapid transit system, supplemented by buses, minibuses, and a cable car. Tbilisi International Airport is the principal gateway to the country.

- Georgia (country)
- Kartli
- List of cities in Georgia

# Maplewood County school board election draws 41 percent turnout

**Turnout more than doubled from the last school board election two years ago**

MAPLEWOOD — Voters in Maplewood County elected three school board members Tuesday in the highest turnout the county has recorded for a stand-alone local race. Election officials said 41 percent of registered voters cast ballots.

The County Elections Office said 38,214 of the district's 93,200 registered voters took part, up from roughly 17 percent two years ago. Lines stretched out the door at several precincts during the after-work rush. The polls at Lincoln Elementary stayed open 25 minutes past the scheduled 7 p.m. closing time so people already waiting could vote.

"We prepared for a busy day, but nothing like this," said Dolores Whitfield, the county's elections director. "By noon we had already surpassed the total in-person turnout from the last cycle."

Six candidates competed for three open seats. The campaign was contentious, with a budget shortfall, school consolidation plans, curriculum and class sizes at the center of it. Spending was unusually large for a local contest, and candidate forums were packed.

Parent groups on both sides of the consolidation debate organized door-knocking and carpools to the polls. In the fall, student volunteers from Maplewood High School ran a registration drive that added nearly 1,800 new voters to the rolls.

"I've lived here 30 years and never voted in a school board race until this year," said Marcus Delgado, 52, a father of two who waited about 20 minutes to vote at Lincoln Elementary. "Decisions about my kids' classrooms are being made, and I wanted a say."

"Closing a school affects the whole neighborhood, not just the families who go there," said Ruth Ann Kessler, a retired teacher.

Preliminary results show incumbent Priya Raman leading, followed by newcomers Thomas Berglund and Angela Ortiz, who currently hold the other two winning positions. Fewer than 400 votes separated third and fourth place. The elections office said final results will not be certified until provisional and mail-in ballots are counted next week.

Whitfield said her office would review the day's operations to prepare for future high-turnout elections. "This is a good problem to have," she said. "We hope it's a sign of lasting engagement."

The new board members will be sworn in at the first meeting of the new year.

Voyager 1

Voyager 1 is a robotic space probe operated by NASA. It was launched on 5 September 1977 as part of the Voyager program to study the outer Solar System. It is now the most distant human-made object from Earth.

The Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) built the probe, and a Titan IIIE rocket carried it from Cape Canaveral, Florida. It launched after its twin, Voyager 2, but took a faster trajectory and reached Jupiter and Saturn first. The mission used a rare planetary alignment that let spacecraft visit several outer planets by gravitational assist.

Voyager 1 reached Jupiter in 1979. It returned detailed images of the planet's atmosphere, including the turbulent cloud bands and the Great Red Spot. On Io it found evidence of active volcanism, the first seen beyond Earth. It also sent back information on Europa, Ganymede, Callisto, Jupiter's magnetosphere, and its ring system.

In 1980 the probe flew past Saturn and its moon Titan. Titan was a major priority because of its dense atmosphere. Voyager 1 confirmed that the atmosphere is rich in nitrogen, but an opaque haze kept it from imaging the surface in detail. It also made extensive observations of Saturn's rings, moons, and magnetic environment. The trajectory required for the Titan flyby sent the spacecraft out of the plane of the Solar System, which ended any chance of further planetary encounters.

After the planetary mission, Voyager 1 began an extended mission to study the outer heliosphere, the region influenced by the solar wind. In August 2012, NASA announced that it had become the first spacecraft to enter interstellar space, crossing the heliopause, where the Sun's influence gives way to the interstellar medium. Its instruments still measure charged particles, magnetic fields, and plasma there.

Voyager 1 carries the Golden Record, a phonograph record of sounds, images, and messages meant to portray the diversity of life and culture on Earth. It was conceived as a symbolic message to any future finders.

Voyager 1 remains in contact with Earth through NASA's Deep Space Network. Its radioisotope thermoelectric generators lose output over time, so its power supply keeps declining. NASA has extended the mission repeatedly, and the probe still returns data as it travels deeper into interstellar space.

Voyager 1

Voyager 1 is a robotic space probe operated by NASA and launched on 5 September 1977 as part of the Voyager program. It was designed primarily to explore the outer Solar System. ## Pivot tables user guide

A pivot table summarizes large sets of spreadsheet data. Instead of sorting, filtering, or writing formulas by hand, you use it to group information, calculate totals, and spot trends.

### When to use a pivot table
Use a pivot table when you want to:
- Total sales by region, product, or salesperson
- Count records, such as customers or orders
- Compare values across categories
- Rearrange data without changing the original table
- Explore patterns in large datasets

### Before you begin
Check that your source data:
- Is organized in rows and columns
- Has a single header row
- Contains no completely blank rows or columns
- Uses consistent data types in each column, such as dates, numbers, or text

Example source columns: `Date`, `Region`, `Product`, `Salesperson`, `Units`, and `Revenue`.

### Creating a pivot table
1. Select any cell in your data range.
2. Open the **Insert** menu and choose **Pivot Table**.
3. Confirm the data range.
4. Choose where to place the pivot table:
   - New worksheet
   - Existing worksheet
5. Click **Create** or **OK**.

A blank pivot table layout and a field list will appear.

### Pivot table areas
Most pivot-table tools have four layout areas:

- **Rows**: displays categories vertically
- **Columns**: displays categories horizontally
- **Values**: shows calculations such as sum, count, or average
- **Filters**: limits the data shown

### Building a basic pivot table
To summarize total revenue by region:
1. Drag **Region** to **Rows**.
2. Drag **Revenue** to **Values**.

The pivot table will show each region with its total revenue.

To compare revenue by region and product:
1. Keep **Region** in **Rows**.
2. Drag **Product** to **Columns**.
3. Keep **Revenue** in **Values**.

### Changing calculations
A value field can often be summarized in different ways, such as:
- Sum
- Count
- Average
- Minimum
- Maximum

To change a calculation:
1. Click the value field in the pivot table or field settings.
2. Open **Value Field Settings** or **Summarize By**.
3. Choose the calculation you want.

### Filtering and sorting
You can refine results by:
- Applying a report filter, such as showing only one year
- Sorting row labels alphabetically or by value
- Expanding or collapsing grouped items

### Refreshing the pivot table
If the source data changes, refresh the pivot table to update the results:
1. Click anywhere in the pivot table.
2. Select **Refresh** from the pivot-table toolbar or context menu.

### Tips
- Use clear column names in your source data
- Format numbers for readability, such as currency or percentages
- If dates do not group correctly, check that they are stored as real dates
- Keep source data unchanged and use the pivot table for analysis

# Pivot Tables

## What Is a Pivot Table?

A pivot table summarizes large datasets without requiring formulas. It lets you group, count, total, and average your data, then rearrange it in seconds to view it from different angles. Use one when you need answers like "What were total sales by region?" or "How many orders did each rep close per month?"

## Before You Begin

Check your data first:

- **Include headers.** Every column needs a unique, nonblank title.
- **Avoid blank rows or columns.** These can cause the table to miss data.
- **Keep data consistent.** Each column should contain one type of information, such as dates or numbers only.

## Creating a Pivot Table

1. Click any cell inside your data range.
2. Open the **Insert** menu and choose **Pivot Table**.
3. Confirm the data range shown is correct.
4. Choose a destination: a new sheet (recommended) or an existing location.
5. Click **OK** or **Create**.

An empty pivot table appears, along with a field panel listing your column headers.

## Understanding the Four Areas

The field panel contains four boxes. Drag fields into them to build your report.

- **Rows:** Categories listed down the left side (for example, Product).
- **Columns:** Categories listed across the top (for example, Quarter).
- **Values:** The numbers being calculated (for example, Sum of Revenue).
- **Filters:** Fields that let you limit the whole table to specific items, such as a single year.

## Example

Suppose your data has columns for Region, Salesperson, Month, and Revenue. To see revenue by region and month:

1. Drag **Region** to Rows.
2. Drag **Month** to Columns.
3. Drag **Revenue** to Values.

The table now shows total revenue for each region-month combination, with grand totals along the edges.

## Changing the Calculation

By default, numeric fields are summed. To change this, click the field in the Values box, select **Value Field Settings**, and choose another function, such as Count, Average, Max, or Min. You can also display values as a percentage of the total.

## Refining Your Report

- **Sort:** Click the dropdown arrow beside a row or column label.
- **Filter:** Use the same arrow to uncheck items you want to hide.
- **Group:** Right-click dates to group them by month, quarter, or year.
- **Rearrange:** Drag fields between areas to see the data differently.

## Keeping Data Current

Pivot tables don't update automatically when source data changes. Right-click the table and select **Refresh**. If you've added new rows, you may need to update the source range under **Change Data Source**.

## Troubleshooting

- **Numbers counted instead of summed:** The column likely contains text or blanks. Clean the data and refresh.
- **Dates won't group:** Some entries may be stored as text. Convert them to true dates.

# What the Walls Remember

When I was nine, my grandmother took me to the train station in the town where she grew up. It had been closed for decades. The windows were clouded and the ticket counter had been stripped of its brass. She pressed her palm flat against the wall of the waiting room, the way you'd check a sleeping animal for breath. "I left for the city from this bench," she said. "Your grandfather proposed on that platform." No architect would have called the building special. Her whole life had swung on it.

I think of that whenever someone says old buildings are obstacles, expensive to maintain and hard to retrofit, standing where something shinier could go. The argument isn't foolish. Old buildings leak, resist wiring, and often fail modern codes, and sentiment won't pay for a new roof. I don't think every old structure deserves rescue. Surviving doesn't make a building sacred.

Some do deserve it, and the reasons are practical as much as sentimental.

Old buildings hold a kind of memory no archive can. A photograph shows how a street looked. A building lets you stand inside proportions people once thought normal. You feel how low the ceilings were and how narrow the stairs, and how much the light came from windows rather than switches. History stops being abstract when you have to duck through its doorway.

They also carry craftsmanship we mostly don't pay for anymore. The library in my hometown, a century-old building I haunted as a teenager, had tiny acorns carved into the banister. Nobody required them, and no budget meeting would approve them today. Generations of restless kids ran their hands over those acorns anyway, and I suspect it taught us that ordinary places could be made with care.

Continuity matters too. A neighborhood built entirely new can feel weightless, like a stage set. Old buildings let a newcomer and a lifelong resident share a landmark, even if they remember it differently. Shared landmarks help hold a community together, and once they're gone they are hard to replace.

Then there is waste. Preservationists like to say the greenest building is the one already standing. Demolition throws away the energy and materials built into it and fills landfills besides.

The train station was torn down for a parking lot. Last year I drove through town and tried to find where the bench had been. I couldn't. The asphalt was smooth, the painted lines were crisp, and nothing suggested that anyone had ever proposed there, or left from there. The bench went with the building, and so did the proof.

The Battle of Hastings was fought on 14 October 1066 between the forces of William, Duke of Normandy, and King Harold Godwinson of England. William won, and the battle decided the Norman Conquest of England. # Transit Strike Halts Buses and Trains, Leaving Thousands of Commuters Stranded

**Union rejects final offer as talks collapse overnight; city braces for second day of disruption**

Hundreds of thousands of commuters scrambled for alternatives Monday after public-transit workers walked off the job at dawn, shutting down bus and rail service across the metropolitan region.

The Metro Transit Workers Union, which represents roughly 8,200 drivers, mechanics, and station staff, began the strike at 4 a.m. after contract negotiations with the Regional Transit Authority broke down late Sunday. It is the first systemwide work stoppage in 14 years.

"We didn't want to be here," said union president Dolores Reyes, speaking from a picket line outside the Eastside bus depot. "But workers who keep this city moving can't be asked to fall behind on rent while costs rise every year."

The union is seeking a 9 percent wage increase over three years, stronger protections against assaults on drivers, and limits on mandatory overtime. Transit officials countered with a 5 percent raise and said they could not meet the remaining demands without raising fares or cutting routes.

"Our offer was fair and fiscally responsible," Authority spokesperson Martin Vail said in a statement. "We remain at the table and urge the union to return to negotiations so riders can get back to their lives."

Highways clogged before sunrise, with traffic officials reporting delays up to 70 percent longer than normal. Ride-share prices surged, and bike-share stations in the downtown core were emptied by 8 a.m. Several major employers encouraged staff to work from home.

At Central Station, normally packed with morning travelers, a handful of people stood reading posted closure notices. Marcus Hill, a hospital cafeteria worker, said he had walked two miles before finding a friend to drive him the rest of the way.

"I support the drivers, I really do," Hill said. "But I can't afford to miss shifts either. I'm stuck in the middle."

Schools reported higher-than-usual absences, and the district said it would keep yellow school buses running, since those are operated by a separate contractor. Paratransit service for riders with disabilities is operating at limited capacity under an emergency agreement, though advocates say wait times have stretched beyond two hours.

Mayor Elaine Cho called on both sides to resume talks immediately and offered city staff as mediators. "Every day this continues costs working families and local businesses," she said.

Economists estimate the shutdown could cost the regional economy $30 million per day in lost productivity and sales.

No new negotiating session has been scheduled. The union said it will continue picketing until it receives a "serious proposal," while the Authority said contingency planning is underway for a prolonged stoppage.

A cracked wall or a faded sign does not become meaningful by surviving, and age alone earns a building nothing. Some buildings are worth keeping anyway, because they hold the craft of the people who made them and a record of how those people pictured their lives. Looking after them keeps a conversation going between generations.

I think of old buildings as public memory. Families keep photo albums, letters, and heirlooms because objects can hold feeling in ways facts cannot, and towns need the same thing. A preserved train station, schoolhouse, or church can tell us more about the people who built a place than any plaque. Look at the width of a staircase, the hand-carved trim around a doorway, the wear in the stone steps. History was lived physically. Someone climbed those stairs every day. Someone stood in that hallway waiting for news or for work, or for grief to pass. When the building goes, part of that memory goes with it.

Many old buildings were made with patience and durable materials, with ornament that reflected pride more than efficiency. Even modest ones show who made them: uneven bricks, wooden floors polished by decades of footsteps, windows placed for grace as well as function. So much construction now is driven by speed and profit, and next to it these buildings show that usefulness and beauty do not have to be enemies.

There is an ethical reason too. Tearing down and rebuilding is not always progress, and sometimes it only means forgetting. Not every old building can or should be saved. Cities have to change, and communities need housing, safety, and accessibility. But when a building has real architectural distinction or deep cultural importance, preserving it is a form of respect. It tells the people who came before us that they are not disposable, and that the struggles and achievements that shaped a neighborhood still count. That matters most for places tied to ordinary people rather than the wealthy or famous. A factory, a corner store, or a union hall may tell a more democratic story than a mansion.

When I walk into an old library or courthouse, I feel for a moment that my own life belongs to a longer story. The building has outlasted fashions and governments and the private worries of everyone who passed through it. It has seen generations come and go, and it still stands. We are not the first people to love a place, and others will come after us who need something solid to remember it by.

Some old buildings deserve preservation not because they are old, but because they continue to matter. A cracked wall or a faded sign does not become meaningful by surviving, and age alone earns a building nothing. But certain buildings carry something larger than themselves: memory, craftsmanship, identity, and the quiet evidence of how people once imagined their lives. # Contributing to the docs

Thanks for helping with the documentation. A typo fix and a new tutorial both make the project easier to use. This guide covers how to get started.

## Ways to contribute

- **Fix errors:** typos, broken links, outdated screenshots, or incorrect code samples.
- **Improve clarity:** rewrite confusing explanations or add missing context.
- **Write new content:** tutorials, how-to guides, and reference pages.
- **Review pull requests:** a reader who is new to a page often spots what its author missed.
- **Report issues:** if you spot a problem but can't fix it, open an issue.

## Getting set up

1. **Fork** the repository and clone your fork locally.
2. Install dependencies with `npm install`.
3. Start the local preview server with `npm run dev`.
4. Open `http://localhost:3000` to see your changes update live.

For small edits, you can also click **Edit this page** at the bottom of any page to make changes directly on GitHub.

## Making a change

1. Create a branch with a descriptive name, such as `fix-install-typo` or `add-auth-guide`.
2. Make your edits in the `docs/` directory. Files are written in Markdown.
3. Run `npm run lint` to check formatting and `npm run build` to confirm the site builds without broken links.
4. Commit with a clear message, such as `Fix incorrect flag in CLI reference`.
5. Push your branch and open a pull request.

## Style guidelines

Please follow these conventions so the docs read consistently:

- **Use plain language.** Prefer short sentences and avoid unnecessary jargon.
- **Address the reader as "you."**
- **Use active voice.** Write "Run the command," not "The command should be run."
- **Put code in code blocks** and specify the language for syntax highlighting.
- **Use sentence case** for headings.
- **Make examples runnable.** Test every snippet before submitting it.
- **Write descriptive link text.** Avoid "click here."

## Structure of the docs

Content falls into four types:

- **Tutorials:** step-by-step lessons for beginners.
- **How-to guides:** solutions to specific problems.
- **Reference:** precise technical descriptions.
- **Explanations:** background and concepts.

Keep each page to one type.

## Pull request checklist

Before submitting, confirm that:

- [ ] The site builds locally without errors.
- [ ] Links and code samples work.
- [ ] Your changes follow the style guidelines.
- [ ] The PR description explains what changed and why.

## Review process

A maintainer usually responds within a few days. They may ask for edits. That's routine and no reflection on your work. Once a PR is approved, it is merged and published automatically.

## Community expectations

Please be kind and patient with each other. All contributors must follow our Code of Conduct.

## Need help?

Ask in our discussion forum or comment on an issue. First-time contributors are welcome to ask.

- Use active voice: write "Run the command," not "The command should be run."
- Put code in code blocks and tag each block with its language.
- Use sentence case for headings.
- Make examples runnable: test every snippet before submitting it.
- Write descriptive link text: avoid "click here."

## Structure of the docs

Content falls into four types:

- Tutorials: step-by-step lessons for beginners.
- How-to guides: solutions to specific problems.
- Reference: precise technical descriptions.
- Explanations: background and concepts.

Keep each page to one type.

## Pull request checklist

Before submitting, confirm that:

- [ ] The site builds locally without errors.
- [ ] Links and code samples work.
- [ ] Your changes follow the style guidelines.
- [ ] The PR description explains what changed and why.

## Review process

A maintainer usually responds within a few days. They may ask for edits. That's routine and no reflection on your work. Once a PR is approved, it is merged and published automatically.

## Community expectations

Please be kind and patient with each other. All contributors must follow our Code of Conduct.

## Need help?

Ask in our discussion forum or comment on an issue. First-time contributors are welcome to ask.

The **Hanseatic League** was a commercial and defensive confederation of merchant guilds and market towns in northwestern and central Europe. From the late 12th to the 17th century it dominated trade on the Baltic and North Seas. At its height it linked nearly 200 towns, from London and Bruges to Novgorod and Bergen.

German merchants, especially from Lübeck and Hamburg, started it by trading abroad and seeking protection and privileges there. Lübeck, founded in 1143 between the North and Baltic Seas, became the League’s leading city. By the 13th century, merchants from German-speaking towns had set up trading outposts called *Kontore* in London, Bruges, Bergen, and Novgorod. Each served as a warehouse and an office, and as a legal community that protected Hanseatic interests.

The League was not a state. It had no formal constitution, permanent army, or central administration; it was a loose association of towns and merchants with shared economic interests. Decisions came out of assemblies called the *Hansetag*, where representatives of member cities negotiated commercial policy, mutual defense, and dealings with foreign rulers. Membership was fluid, and some cities took part far more than others.

Its economic power rested on the exchange of regional goods. The east sent grain, timber, wax, fur, and fish; the west and south sent cloth, wine, salt, and metal goods. Hanseatic merchants built efficient shipping networks and standardized commercial practices, which lowered transaction costs and increased trust over long distances. When necessary, the League used embargoes and naval force to defend its privileges, as in its conflicts with Denmark in the 14th century.

The decline began in the late 15th century and was gradual. Stronger territorial states, trade routes shifting toward the Atlantic, Dutch and English competition, and divisions among the members all weakened it. Overseas privileges were cut back step by step, and several *Kontore* closed. Some cities still identified with the League, but by the 17th century its political weight was gone. The *Hansetag* last met in 1669.

Lübeck, Hamburg, Bremen, and Tallinn, all former Hanseatic cities, still have brick Gothic buildings and civic traditions associated with the League. It also influenced the commercial law of northern Europe.

# Bike-Share FAQ

## Getting Started

**How do I rent a bike?**
Download our app and create an account. Then find a nearby station, tap "Unlock," and scan the QR code on the bike. You can also unlock bikes at station kiosks using a credit card.

**How much does it cost?**
- **Single ride:** $1 to unlock, plus $0.15 per minute
- **Day pass:** $12, with unlimited 30-minute rides for 24 hours
- **Monthly membership:** $20, with unlimited 45-minute rides
- **Annual membership:** $150, with unlimited 45-minute rides

Discounted memberships are available for students, seniors, and low-income residents. Visit our website to apply.

## Using the Service

**How long can I keep a bike?**
Ride as long as you like, but time beyond your plan's included minutes is billed at $0.15 per minute. For longer trips, dock the bike and check out another to reset your time.

**Where can I return my bike?**
Return it to any station with an open dock. Push the front wheel firmly into the dock until the light turns green. If a station is full, use the app to find the nearest one with space, and you'll receive a free 10-minute extension.

**Do I need to bring a helmet?**
Helmets aren't provided, but we strongly recommend wearing one. Riders under 16 are required by law to wear a helmet.

**Are electric bikes available?**
Yes. E-bikes are marked with a green stripe and cost an additional $0.10 per minute. They assist you up to 20 mph.

## Safety and Problems

**What if a bike is damaged?**
Check the brakes, tires, and seat before riding. If something seems wrong, press the red "Report" button on the bike's screen or use the app. Then return it to a dock to take it out of service. You won't be charged for rides under one minute.

**What if the bike is lost or stolen?**
Lock the bike with the built-in cable lock whenever you pause. Use the "Hold" feature in the app for short stops. If a bike is lost or stolen while in your care, report it within 24 hours. Unreported losses may result in a $250 fee.

**Can I ride at night?**
Yes. Our bikes have built-in front and rear lights that activate automatically.

## Account Help

**Can I share my membership?**
No. Memberships are personal, and each account can only unlock one bike at a time. Group rides require multiple accounts.

**How do I cancel my membership?**
Go to Settings > Membership in the app and select "Cancel." Monthly plans end at the close of the billing period, and annual plans can be refunded within 14 days.

**Who do I contact for help?**
Call 555-0142, email help@citybikeshare.example, or use the in-app chat. Support is available daily from 6 a.m. to 10 p.m.

## Plugin system

The editor has a plugin system for extending it without modifying the main application. A plugin can add commands, sidebar panels, language support, formatters, themes, and event-driven behavior.

### Plugin structure

Each plugin lives in its own directory and needs a manifest file named `plugin.json`. A typical plugin looks like this:

```text
my-plugin/
  plugin.json
  main.js
  README.md
  assets/
```

The `plugin.json` file holds the plugin's metadata and entry point:

```json
{
  "id": "example.hello-world",
  "name": "Hello World",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "main": "main.js",
  "enabled": true
}
```

Required fields:

- `id`: Unique plugin identifier.
- `name`: Human-readable name.
- `version`: Plugin version.
- `main`: Entry script loaded by the editor.

Optional fields include `description`, `author`, and `dependencies`.

### Lifecycle

On startup, the editor scans the plugin directory, reads each manifest, and loads the enabled plugins. The entry script must export an `activate` function. It can also export a `deactivate` function, which the editor calls when the plugin is unloaded or the editor exits.

Example:

```js
export function activate(api) {
  api.commands.register("hello.sayHello", () => {
    api.window.showMessage("Hello from plugin!");
  });
}

export function deactivate() {
  // Clean up resources here
}
```

Register commands, subscribe to events, and initialize UI elements in `activate`. Dispose of timers, listeners, and temporary state in `deactivate`.

### Editor API

The `api` object passed to `activate` is how a plugin talks to the editor. Commonly used namespaces:

- `api.commands`: Register and execute commands.
- `api.window`: Show notifications, dialogs, and UI panels.
- `api.workspace`: Access open files, project folders, and settings.
- `api.editor`: Read or modify the active document.
- `api.events`: Subscribe to editor events such as file open, save, or cursor movement.

Example command registration:

```js
export function activate(api) {
  api.commands.register("example.insertDate", () => {
    const editor = api.editor.getActiveEditor();
    if (!editor) return;

    editor.insertText(new Date().toLocaleDateString());
  });
}
```

### Installation and management

To install a plugin, copy its directory into the editor's `plugins/` folder or use the built-in plugin manager. The settings interface lets you enable, disable, update, or remove plugins.

If a plugin fails to load, the editor logs the error and keeps starting up. Load errors, activation failures, and dependency issues show up in the developer console.

### Best practices

- Give each plugin one responsibility.
- Use stable, namespaced command IDs such as `author.feature.action`.
- Validate settings, and handle missing editor state gracefully.
- Dispose of event listeners during deactivation.
- Avoid blocking operations during activation so startup stays fast.

# On being bored

Last summer my phone died on a train, and I had four hours of countryside ahead of me and only the window to look at. For the first twenty minutes I was nearly frantic. My hand kept going to my pocket like a tongue to a missing tooth. I counted fence posts. I reread the safety instructions above the door. I was bored, plainly.

Then it shifted. Somewhere past a river I couldn't name, my mind quit scrambling for input and began making its own. I remembered a conversation with my grandmother that I hadn't thought of in years. I worked out how to restructure a project at work that had nagged at me for weeks. For no reason at all, I invented an elaborate backstory for the man asleep across the aisle. **The Weight of a Hamburger**

When I was nine, I watched my uncle slaughter a pig. I had been told to stay in the truck, and of course I didn't. I don't remember the blood. I remember the quiet afterward, and how ordinary the men became once it was done, rinsing their hands and talking about the weather. That night we ate pork shoulder. It was delicious, and I could not stop thinking about the pig's eyes.

I've been circling that evening for most of my adult life.

For years I avoided the question the way you avoid a bill you suspect you can't pay. I ate chicken breasts that came in plastic, shaped like nothing that had ever lived. Then I read a book about industrial farming, one of those books written to ruin your appetite, and it did. I was a vegetarian for three years, sincere and a little insufferable.

I believed then, and still believe, that suffering matters. Pigs are intelligent and social, and they feel fear. If a dog's pain counts for something, I have to explain why a pig's doesn't, and "because it tastes good" is a poor argument. Most of the world's meat comes from animals that lived in conditions I would call cruel if I saw them applied to anything I loved. I can't argue around that, and I've stopped trying.

My certainty has worn down since, though the arguments haven't gotten any weaker. Life got more complicated. I spent a winter with relatives who ate largely what they raised and hunted, and their relationship to meat was nothing like mine. They knew the animals, thanked them without embarrassment, and wasted nothing. I couldn't honestly say they were doing something worse than I was, standing in a grocery aisle buying almond milk shipped from a drought-stricken valley. Every way of eating costs something.

I've landed somewhere uncomfortable. What bothers me most about modern meat is how thoroughly the killing has been hidden from us. Distance makes cruelty easy. If I'm going to eat an animal, I should be willing to know where it lived and how it was killed. If I can't stand to know, that's information too.

So now I eat meat rarely and try to know its source. I buy from a farmer whose fields I've walked through. Sometimes I fail and eat the convenient thing at an airport or a wedding, and I feel the old pang. I don't think this makes me virtuous. Maybe it just makes me a more thoughtful participant in something I can't fully justify.

I used to want a clean answer, a rule to follow or a principle that would let me stop thinking. I distrust that wish now.

I still think about the pig sometimes. I take the memory to mean that I should stay awake while I eat.

Svalbard Global Seed Vault

The Svalbard Global Seed Vault is a seed storage facility on Spitsbergen, in Norway's Svalbard archipelago, about 1,300 kilometres from the North Pole. It opened in 2008 to hold duplicate samples of seeds from gene banks around the world, so that crop diversity survives if a collection is lost to war, natural disaster, equipment failure, climate change, or poor management.

The vault is built into the side of Platåberget, a sandstone mountain near the settlement of Longyearbyen. The remote Arctic site was chosen for political and environmental reasons. Svalbard is geologically stable, and the cold climate and surrounding permafrost help keep the seeds frozen if the power fails. Seeds are stored at about −18 °C (0 °F), a standard temperature for long-term storage in seed banks.

It is sometimes called the "doomsday vault." It is a backup repository, not a conventional seed bank. The vault does not own the seeds deposited there. Under a "black box" arrangement they remain the property of the depositing institutions, and only the depositors can access their collections. The aim is to give national, regional, and international gene banks an additional layer of security.

The Government of Norway developed the vault in partnership with the Nordic Genetic Resource Center (NordGen) and the Crop Trust. It can store millions of seed samples from food crops and their wild relatives, including wheat, rice, maize, barley, beans, and many other agriculturally important species. That diversity is a resource for plant breeding, food security, and adaptation to changing environmental conditions.

In 2015, the International Center for Agricultural Research in the Dry Areas (ICARDA) became the first institution to withdraw seeds from the vault. Conflict in Syria had disrupted operations at its regional gene bank. ICARDA used the withdrawn seeds to regenerate its collections and later deposited fresh samples.

**The Weight of Paper**

After my grandmother died, I found her letters in a shoebox, rubber-banded by year. Mine were in there too, dutiful childhood notes about school and a lost tooth, which she had kept for decades. But it was her side of the correspondence I couldn't stop reading, the letters my mother had saved and passed back to me.

Nothing happens in them. The tomatoes are coming in late. Mrs. Dolan's hip is no better. It rained Tuesday, then Wednesday, then, she wrote, "it seemed to lose interest." I laughed out loud at that, alone in my kitchen, hearing her dry voice come through the slanted blue ink. She had crossed out a word and written another above it, and I could see her hesitate and decide. That small correction told me more about her than any photograph.

What we lose when we stop writing letters is evidence of attention. A letter proves that someone sat down and held you in mind for twenty uninterrupted minutes, not while waiting for coffee or half-watching television. They chose a page, a pen, and you. Now I send dozens of messages a day, and they are quick and useful but weightless. They arrive mid-distraction and are answered mid-distraction. Almost none of them are kept.

Letters also demanded patience, and the patience shaped what people said. You couldn't fire off a feeling and retract it ten seconds later. You had to let a thought finish itself, and sometimes in the finishing it changed. My grandfather, I learned from the shoebox, once wrote three pages to my grandmother about a quarrel, and the last paragraph contradicts the first. He hadn't meant to forgive her when he began. The letter got him there. A text would have kept him angry, or ended the argument in a single clipped word.

Then there was the waiting. We treat waiting as pure cost now, a flaw to be engineered away. But the days between sending and receiving gave longing somewhere to live. You walked to the mailbox with a small, private hope. When something came, it had traveled to reach you. It had a smudge on it and a faint smell of someone else's house.

Last winter I wrote a letter to an old friend who had moved across the country. It took me an hour and a half, far longer than I expected, because I kept discovering things I hadn't realized I wanted to say. My handwriting had gone ragged from disuse. I crossed out a word and wrote another above it. When I dropped the envelope in the box, I felt oddly exposed, as though I'd handed over something I couldn't edit.

She wrote back three weeks later. I have it still, on my desk, the paper slightly creased where her hand pressed down. It says, among other things, that it has been raining, and that the rain seems to have lost interest.

# Design Proposal: Caching Layer for Web API

## Overview
This proposal adds a caching layer to the web API to cut response latency and backend load, so the API can handle more traffic. The cache stores responses to frequently requested calls and serves them without another trip to the database or downstream services.

## Goals
- Reduce average API response time
- Lower database and service load
- Improve throughput during traffic spikes
- Keep data fresh enough for each endpoint
- Show how the cache behaves

## Non-Goals
- Replacing the primary database
- Caching highly sensitive or user-specific data without additional controls
- Guaranteeing fresh data on every endpoint

## Architecture
The cache sits between the API application and the backend data sources. The API checks the cache first, and a valid entry is returned immediately. On a miss, the API fetches from the source, returns the response, and writes it to the cache.

We recommend a distributed in-memory store such as Redis: it has low latency, supports expiration, and is mature to operate. A CDN or edge cache could be added later for static or public GET endpoints.

## Cache Strategy
The first version uses **cache-aside**:
1. Client requests resource
2. API looks up cache key
3. On hit, return cached response
4. On miss, fetch from backend
5. Store result in cache with TTL
6. Return response

It is simple and works well for read-heavy workloads.

## Key Design
Cache keys must be deterministic and include:
- Endpoint path
- Normalized query parameters
- API version
- Relevant request context such as locale

Example:

`v1:products:list:category=books:page=2:locale=en-US`

## Expiration and Invalidation
Each cached item gets a TTL set by how often its endpoint's data changes:
- Reference data: 1–24 hours
- Frequently updated entities: 1–5 minutes
- Aggregated results: 30–120 seconds

Writes that affect a cached resource should invalidate it. When a product is updated, for example, its detail and listing keys should be deleted or versioned. Where exact invalidation is hard, use a shorter TTL.

## Reliability Considerations
To avoid cache stampedes, use request coalescing or a soft TTL with background refresh. Known missing resources can be cached briefly as misses, which cuts repeated lookups. If the cache is down, the API must fall back to the backend.

## Security
Don't cache sensitive data unless it is encrypted and scoped per user. Public and shared caches must exclude authenticated or personalized responses by default.

## Observability
Metrics:
- Cache hit rate
- Miss rate
- Eviction rate
- Latency by endpoint
- Backend request reduction

Add structured logs and dashboards so the team can see whether the cache is working.

## Rollout Plan
Start with a few GET endpoints that are read often and change rarely. Measure hit rate and latency, then expand gradually. Rolling out in phases keeps the risk small and shows what the cache does under real traffic.

Library of Alexandria

The Library of Alexandria was a major center of scholarship in Alexandria, Egypt, during the Hellenistic period. It was associated with the Mouseion ("Temple of the Muses"), a research institution the Ptolemaic dynasty established after the conquests of Alexander the Great. Many details remain uncertain, and the library has become a symbol of learning and of cultural loss.

The library was probably founded in the early 3rd century BCE, most likely under Ptolemy I Soter or his son Ptolemy II Philadelphus. The Ptolemies wanted Alexandria to be the leading center of Greek culture and scholarship, so they collected texts from across the Mediterranean world: literature, philosophy, science, mathematics, and history. Ancient sources describe an aggressive acquisition policy. Books arriving in the city were reportedly copied, and in some cases the library kept the originals and returned the copies to their owners.

Scholars working there edited and compared texts, and their work helped establish critical editions of Greek authors such as Homer. Euclid, Eratosthenes, Aristarchus of Samothrace, and Callimachus were all associated with the institution. Callimachus is traditionally credited with compiling the Pinakes, a large bibliographic catalogue often regarded as one of the earliest library catalogues.

Estimates of the library's size vary widely. Ancient and modern figures range from tens of thousands to several hundred thousand scrolls. Historians also debate how the library was organized and how it related to a possible "daughter library" in the Serapeum.

The library's destruction is among the best-known episodes in cultural history, but it likely did not happen in a single catastrophic event. Ancient and later sources connect its decline to several episodes: Julius Caesar's campaign in Alexandria in 48 BCE, political turmoil in the Roman period, and the destruction of pagan institutions in late antiquity, especially during the 4th century CE. Modern historians generally conclude that the library diminished gradually over centuries rather than being suddenly destroyed.

It has come to represent universal knowledge and the fragility of cultural memory. The Bibliotheca Alexandrina, inaugurated in modern Alexandria in 2002, was conceived as a tribute to the ancient library.

# Hanseatic League

The **Hanseatic League** (also known as the **Hansa**) was a commercial and defensive confederation of merchant guilds and market towns in Northern and Central Europe. It originated in the 12th century, reached its height between the 13th and 15th centuries, and dominated trade across the Baltic Sea and North Sea regions. Its member cities lay mainly along the coasts of present-day Germany, Poland, the Baltic states, and neighboring regions.

## Origins

The League emerged from associations of German merchants who traveled together for protection against piracy and banditry. The founding of Lübeck in 1143 and its rise as a gateway to the Baltic were central to this. Lübeck's 1241 agreement with Hamburg is often cited as an early step. Many other towns later joined, including Cologne, Bremen, Danzig (Gdańsk), Riga, and Tallinn (Reval).

## Organization

The Hansa was never a state in the modern sense. It had no standing army, permanent treasury, or formal constitution. It was a loose association governed by periodic assemblies called the *Hansetag*, which met mainly in Lübeck. Decisions were enforced through collective economic pressure, such as trade embargoes, and occasionally through military action. Lübeck is generally regarded as the League's leading city, often called its "Queen."

## Trade

Hanseatic merchants traded in bulk commodities. From the east they carried timber, furs, wax, amber, grain, and rye; from the west and south they brought cloth, wine, and manufactured goods. Salted herring from Scania and salt from Lüneburg were also key goods. The League maintained overseas trading posts, known as *Kontore*, in London (the Steelyard), Bruges, Bergen, and Novgorod (the Peterhof). These enclaves had special privileges and operated under their own rules.

## Conflicts

The Hansa's power brought it into conflict with rulers who resented its trading privileges. The largest conflict was a war with Denmark, which ended with the Treaty of Stralsund in 1370 and confirmed Hanseatic dominance in the Baltic. Later, competition from Dutch, English, and Scandinavian merchants steadily eroded its position.

## Decline

From the late 15th century the League weakened as territorial states grew stronger, trade routes shifted toward the Atlantic, Dutch commercial power rose, and the members failed to hold together. The loss of key privileges, such as the closure of the Steelyard in London in 1598, cut its influence further. The last formal assembly took place in 1669, though Lübeck, Hamburg, and Bremen kept the Hanseatic name for centuries.

## Legacy

The League left brick Gothic buildings across the Baltic. Hamburg and Bremen still use "Free and Hanseatic City" in their official titles. The "New Hanse" and the annual Hanseatic Days still commemorate it.

The Dust Bowl was a period of severe dust storms and ecological disaster on the Great Plains in the 1930s, worst from 1934 to 1936. Prolonged drought and high winds hit soil that poor farming practices had left open to erosion. Oklahoma, Texas, Kansas, Colorado, and New Mexico suffered most.

Deep-rooted native grasses once covered much of the Great Plains and held the soil in place. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, large areas of prairie were plowed for wheat farming and cattle grazing. High crop prices and the belief that "rain follows the plow" pushed many farmers onto marginal land. Then the drought arrived in the early 1930s. The bare topsoil dried out, and strong winds lifted it with ease.

The dust storms were the most visible sign of the disaster. Sometimes called "black blizzards," they carried enormous clouds of soil over towns, farms, and distant cities. On April 14, 1935, a day remembered as Black Sunday, a massive wall of dust swept across the southern Plains. The storms destroyed crops, buried machinery, and killed livestock. They also contributed to widespread respiratory problems known as "dust pneumonia."

The Dust Bowl made the Great Depression harder to bear. Farm incomes collapsed, banks failed, and many families lost their land. Hundreds of thousands of people left the Plains for California and other western states, looking for work and better living conditions, especially from Oklahoma and Arkansas. They were often called "Okies," though many came from other states. John Steinbeck's *The Grapes of Wrath* later depicted their experiences.

The federal government answered with conservation and relief programs under President Franklin D. Roosevelt's New Deal. The Soil Conservation Service, established in 1935, promoted farming methods that reduced erosion: contour plowing, crop rotation, strip farming, and shelterbelts of trees. Other programs helped struggling farm families relocate or stay on their land.

Rainfall gradually returned in the late 1930s and eased the worst conditions. The Dust Bowl remains one of the most significant environmental disasters in U.S. history, and it is still cited as a warning about unsustainable land use and the vulnerability of agriculture to ecological change.

# The Friendship That Lives in My Pocket

When I was twelve, my best friend moved across the country and we wrote letters. They were clumsy, full of crossed-out words and drawings in the margins. A reply took two weeks, sometimes three. I got a small thrill from seeing her handwriting in the mailbox, and I read each letter so many times that the folds went soft. We lost touch within a year. Distance did that then.

My own kids won't know that kind of loss. I'm still deciding how I feel about it.

Social media has changed what friendship means, and I notice it most when I try to explain it. I know what my college roommate had for dinner last night. I know her daughter lost a tooth, that her mother has been ill, that she's frustrated with her job. I haven't spoken to her in four years. Is she my friend? By the old definition, probably not. By the new one she's someone I "keep up with," a category that means closeness without contact.

It has given me some real things. I've watched friendships survive moves and career changes and the ordinary drift that used to end them. A friend in another time zone sends me voice memos while she walks her dog, and I answer while I do dishes. It isn't the same as sitting across from her, but it counts for something. Threads can be pulled tight again, and when we finally see each other, we don't start from zero.

The costs are quieter, and I've felt them more as I've gotten older. Friendship starts to feel like a performance with an audience. I've caught myself composing a moment while I'm still inside it, angling the dinner table for a photo, thinking of a caption while a friend is mid-sentence. Somewhere in there the person across from me turns into a co-star.

Affection has gotten cheap too. A like costs nothing. A birthday message from a platform's reminder takes four seconds. We send these tokens and feel we've done the caring, when real friendship has always asked for something less efficient: showing up, sitting in awkward silence, driving across town when someone's life falls apart. No app automated that. It only made us feel we didn't need to.

Last winter, a friend I'd only ever "liked" from afar posted something vague and sad. I almost scrolled past. Instead I called her. We talked for two hours and she cried, and I realized how long it had been since I'd heard her actual voice. The post was a small flare, and I'd nearly taken it for scenery.

So here is where I've ended up. Social media gave me more people to reach and less to hold each of them with. Whether the feed is the friendship or only a doorway into one is up to us.

I still have her old letters, soft at the folds. I wouldn't go back to waiting three weeks for a reply. But I'd like to write like that again, slowly, with crossed-out words, meaning every one.

By Thursday afternoon the office feels different. People are still answering email, sitting in meetings, and updating spreadsheets, but the sharpness of Monday is gone. Conversations drift. Small tasks take longer than they should. By Friday it sometimes seems that everyone is acting out work rather than doing it. That feeling has made me more sympathetic to a four-day week.

The extra day to sleep in is nice, but it is not what persuades me. What does is the idea that more hours at work do not always produce better work. In office jobs especially, output does not track hours logged. Attention runs out. Creativity fades with overuse. Tired people decide badly. We talk as if endurance were the top professional virtue, yet clarity matters more than duration. A shorter week admits that people are not machines, and treating them like machines gets mediocre results.

I like the idea, too, because it treats rest as worth having instead of as indulgence. In many workplaces exhaustion is a badge of honor: being overwhelmed means being important, being unavailable means being needed. That logic feels hollow to me. Rest does not oppose responsibility. It is one of the things that makes responsibility possible. An extra day off could go to recovering, looking after children or parents, booking a doctor's appointment without stress, reading, exercising, or just living outside the reach of employers and inboxes. People with room for a fuller life tend to come back to work more focused and less resentful.

There is also a moral argument, I think. For generations, new technology was sold as a route to efficiency and freedom. For many workers the efficiency never became leisure. It became higher expectations. We can answer messages instantly, produce documents faster, and automate routine tasks, and the reward is often more work. A four-day week offers another outcome: the gains from innovation could finally be paid out in time.

Of course, not every profession can adopt the same schedule the same way. Hospitals, schools, factories, and service industries have practical constraints. A four-day week will not fix every workplace problem. It needs careful implementation, staffing changes, and a real commitment not to cram five days of meetings into four. But those challenges do not weaken the idea. They are a reason to rethink old assumptions.

For me, this comes down to dignity. Should work consume the best of our lives, or support it? I do not think people want to contribute less. I think they want to contribute in a way they can keep up, and still have something left of themselves for the rest of life.

A four-day week will not fix every workplace problem. It needs careful implementation, staffing changes, and a real commitment not to cram five days of meetings into four. But those challenges do not weaken the idea. They are a reason to rethink old assumptions.

For me, this comes down to dignity. Should work consume the best of our lives, or support it? I do not think people want to contribute less. I think they want to contribute in a way they can keep up, and still have something left of themselves for the rest of life.

# Wildfire Forces Thousands to Evacuate Near Cedar Ridge National Park

**CEDAR FALLS, Mont.** — A fast-moving wildfire tore through dry timber along the western edge of Cedar Ridge National Park on Tuesday, forcing the evacuation of more than 3,000 residents and prompting officials to close the park to all visitors.

The blaze, named the Hollow Creek Fire, was first reported shortly after 2 p.m. Monday and has since burned an estimated 14,000 acres. Fire officials said it was zero percent contained as of Wednesday morning.

"This fire is moving faster than anything we've seen in this area in a decade," said Incident Commander Dana Whitfield at an evening briefing. "Dry fuels, low humidity, and gusting winds are all working against us."

Mandatory evacuation orders were issued for the communities of Pine Hollow, Larkspur, and parts of Cedar Falls. An additional 2,000 residents in neighboring areas were told to be ready to leave on short notice. Sheriff's deputies went door to door overnight, and emergency alerts were sent to cell phones throughout the county.

An evacuation center opened at Cedar Falls High School, where the Red Cross provided cots, meals, and information. By midday, more than 400 people had checked in. Many arrived with pets, medications, and little else.

"We had about fifteen minutes to grab what we could," said Maria Delgado, a Larkspur resident who left with her two children and their dog. "I took photo albums, documents, and clothes. You just hope the house is still there when you get back."

Park Superintendent Tom Ellery said all campgrounds and trails had been cleared and that rangers had accounted for all registered backcountry visitors. "Visitor safety is our top priority," he said. "We are also working closely with firefighters to protect historic structures, including the Ridgeline Lodge, which dates to 1932."

More than 600 firefighters, supported by helicopters and air tankers, are battling the flames. Crews have focused on building containment lines near homes and protecting power infrastructure. Two firefighters suffered minor heat-related injuries, officials said. No civilian injuries or deaths have been reported.

Smoke has drifted across the region, and health officials issued air quality warnings for three counties, urging children, older adults, and people with respiratory conditions to stay indoors.

Meteorologists said there is a slight chance of rain late Friday, though thunderstorms could also bring dangerous lightning and erratic winds.

Governor Elaine Parks declared a state of emergency Tuesday, freeing up additional state resources. Officials have not determined the cause of the fire, and an investigation is underway.

Residents can find updates and shelter information on the county emergency management website.

# The Weight of Boxes

What I noticed first about my new city was the silence, which was louder than I expected. In my old apartment I knew every sound: the radiator's knock, the upstairs neighbor's heavy footsteps, the bus that groaned past at 6:40 each morning. Here, in a sublet that smelled faintly of someone else's cooking, I lay awake listening to noises I couldn't name.

Moving is a small, voluntary amnesia. I had lived in my old city for nine years and could navigate it half asleep. I knew which grocery store stocked good tomatoes, which streets flooded in spring, which barista would start my order when I walked in. In the new city I got lost on the way to the pharmacy, and I stood in the cereal aisle for ten minutes, undone by brands I didn't recognize. At thirty-four, I felt like a child. It was humbling and a little absurd.

The humbling turned out to help. Within a week my attention had sharpened in a way it hadn't in years. I noticed the brick on my street, a warm rust that glowed at dusk. I noticed that people here nodded at strangers. I took the long way everywhere, since I had no short way yet. A city you don't know makes you look at it, and looking, I realized, is a pleasure I'd stopped practicing. Routine had been quietly sanding my days down until they all felt the same.

There were smaller delights. A bakery owner began saving me the end pieces of the rye loaf. On Sunday mornings a river path let runners and old men with fishing rods share the same few feet of asphalt in peaceful disregard. No one had told me about either place. I found them by wandering.

The costs were real too. One Tuesday something funny happened and I reached for my phone to tell a friend, then did the math on time zones and put it down. In the quiet of the second month, when the novelty thinned, I understood that friendship can't be unpacked like a box. It builds slowly, through repetition and accident, through being around. I had traded people who knew my history for people who knew only my present, and that is lonelier than I'd expected.

I've been here a year now. The bus no longer sounds foreign. I have a tomato place. Last month a woman at the bakery asked how my week was going, and I realized I had a week worth describing. I still miss the old city, the way you miss a language you used to speak well.

Homesickness, I've come to think, is the price of having loved a place, and paying it isn't a mistake. Moving showed me I could be rebuilt, that I was more portable than I'd feared. The boxes are long gone.

# Dust Bowl

The **Dust Bowl**, also known as the **Dirty Thirties**, was a period of severe dust storms that caused major ecological and agricultural damage to the American and Canadian prairie lands during the 1930s. Severe drought and decades of farming without techniques to prevent wind erosion, such as crop rotation, cover crops, and terracing, caused the storms.

## Background

During the late 19th and early 20th centuries, settlers moved onto the Great Plains in large numbers, encouraged by the Homestead Acts and by unusually wet weather in the early 1900s. The native deep-rooted prairie grasses were plowed under to plant wheat. High wheat prices during and after World War I accelerated this expansion, and gasoline-powered tractors and combines let farmers cultivate far more land than before. Millions of acres of grassland were converted to cropland, leaving the soil exposed.

## Drought and storms

A series of droughts began in 1930 and recurred in waves through 1936 and 1939–1940. With the grasses that once anchored the soil gone, high winds lifted the dry topsoil into enormous clouds. The most severe region included the panhandles of Texas and Oklahoma, as well as parts of western Kansas, eastern Colorado, and northeastern New Mexico.

On **April 14, 1935**, remembered as "Black Sunday," a massive storm carried dust across the southern plains, turning day into night. The following day, journalist Robert Geiger used the term "Dust Bowl" in a news dispatch, and the name stuck. Some storms carried dust as far as Washington, D.C., and ships in the Atlantic Ocean.

## Human impact

The storms damaged crops, buried farm equipment, and killed livestock. Many residents developed "dust pneumonia" and other respiratory illnesses. Combined with the economic hardship of the Great Depression, the crisis forced many families to leave their farms. Roughly 3.5 million people moved out of the Plains states in the 1930s, many of them to California. John Steinbeck's novel *The Grapes of Wrath* (1939), Dorothea Lange's photographs, and Woody Guthrie's songs recorded their experiences.

## Government response

The federal government established programs to address the crisis. The Soil Conservation Service, created in 1935 under Hugh Hammond Bennett, promoted soil-saving techniques including contour plowing, strip cropping, and crop rotation. The Prairie States Forestry Project, begun in 1934, planted millions of trees across the Plains as windbreaks known as shelterbelts. The Taylor Grazing Act of 1934 also regulated grazing on public lands.

## Legacy

Rainfall returned in late 1939, ending the drought. The Dust Bowl remains one of the worst environmental disasters in American history. It shaped the soil conservation policy and farming practices that followed.

The Erie Canal is a canal in New York State that opened in 1825. It gave boats a water route from the Hudson River at Albany to Lake Erie at Buffalo, connecting the Atlantic Ocean to the Great Lakes. Shipping costs fell, settlers moved west faster, and New York City became the country's leading port.

The canal was proposed in the early 19th century because moving goods and people across the Appalachians was slow, expensive, and often unreliable. Governor DeWitt Clinton became its leading political advocate, and critics sometimes mocked the project as "Clinton's Ditch." Construction began in 1817. Thousands of laborers, many of them immigrants, cut through forests, dug trenches, and built aqueducts and locks over difficult terrain.

The original canal was about 363 miles (584 km) long, 40 feet (12 m) wide, and 4 feet (1.2 m) deep. Its 83 locks handled an elevation difference of more than 500 feet (150 m) between the Hudson and Lake Erie. It officially opened on October 26, 1825. Clinton marked the day with the "Wedding of the Waters," a ceremonial journey from Buffalo to New York Harbor, where water from Lake Erie was poured into the Atlantic.

Freight rates between the Midwest and the East Coast fell sharply, so shipping farm products, raw materials, and manufactured goods cost much less. Syracuse, Rochester, Utica, and Buffalo grew rapidly. The canal also drew migrants to western New York, Ohio, Indiana, and other parts of the Old Northwest.

The canal was enlarged several times during the 19th century. In the early 20th century, much of the original route became part of the New York State Barge Canal System, which opened in 1918 and combined canalized rivers with new canal cuts. Railroads and highways later took much of the commercial traffic.

Today the canal is used mainly for recreation, tourism, and heritage purposes.
