# Voyager 1

**Voyager 1** is a space probe launched by NASA on September 5, 1977, as part of the Voyager program to study the outer Solar System and interstellar space. It launched sixteen days after its twin, Voyager 2. It is the most distant human-made object from Earth, moving at roughly 17 kilometers per second (about 61,000 km/h) relative to the Sun.

## Mission background

The outer planets line up in a rare alignment about once every 175 years, and the Voyager program used it. The alignment let spacecraft take gravity assists from one planet to the next. NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) built the probes and originally funded a four-year mission to Jupiter and Saturn.

## Spacecraft design

Voyager 1 had a mass of about 825 kilograms at launch. It communicates with the Deep Space Network through a 3.7-meter high-gain antenna. Three radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs) supply power by converting heat from decaying plutonium-238 into electricity. Their output falls by several watts each year, so engineers have gradually switched off nonessential instruments and heaters. The spacecraft also carries the Golden Record, a gold-plated phonograph record of sounds, images, and music from life and culture on Earth.

## Planetary encounters

Voyager 1 made its closest approach to Jupiter on March 5, 1979, and found active volcanism on the moon Io, the first volcanic activity observed beyond Earth. It reached Saturn on November 12, 1980, and sent back detailed images of the rings and of the largest moon, Titan, whose thick atmosphere was studied closely. The Titan flyby bent the probe's trajectory out of the ecliptic plane and ended its planetary tour. In 1990, it took the "Family Portrait" of the Solar System, which includes the image of Earth known as the *Pale Blue Dot*.

## Interstellar mission

On August 25, 2012, Voyager 1 crossed the heliopause, where the Sun's solar wind gives way to the interstellar medium, and became the first spacecraft to enter interstellar space. Its plasma wave instrument measured a sharp rise in plasma density that confirmed the crossing.

In November 2023, a fault in one of the onboard computers caused the probe to begin sending unintelligible data. JPL engineers traced it to a corrupted memory chip in the flight data subsystem. In 2024 they restored communication by relocating the affected code. The spacecraft was then more than 24 billion kilometers away.

## Future

Voyager 1 still transmits data on magnetic fields, cosmic rays, and plasma. Mission planners expect the RTGs to power at least one instrument into the mid-2020s, possibly longer. After that the probe will keep drifting through the Milky Way. In roughly 40,000 years it will pass within about 1.6 light-years of the star Gliese 445.

## See also

- Voyager 2
- Voyager program
- Pioneer 10
- Golden Record

# The Last Free Room

When I was nine, my family moved to a new town in the middle of winter, and for weeks I knew no one. My mother worked two jobs. My father was still in our old city, finishing out a lease. The apartment was small and quiet, and the afternoons were long. One day I followed a stranger's dog down the street and ended up in front of the public library.

It turned out to be the one place in town that wanted nothing from me.

I think about that now, as an adult who knows how rare it is. Almost everywhere else, taking up space means buying something. Coffee shops want a latte. Malls want a receipt. Even parks have rules and hours. The library says: come in, sit down, stay as long as you like. It may be the last truly free room in American life, and I suspect we undervalue it because it asks so little.

People argue that libraries are obsolete because everything is online. That misunderstands what a library is. It lends books, which is a small miracle on its own: one copy of a novel can pass through fifty hands. But watch a library for an afternoon and you'll see it doing far more. A man in a worn jacket fills out a job application on a public computer while a librarian patiently helps him attach his résumé. A teenager does homework because her home has no internet. A toddler learns to sit through a story. Someone gets help with tax forms, someone else is learning English, and someone is simply warm, out of the cold, safe for a few hours. The library treats every one of them as a citizen.

Its central premise is radical: knowledge shouldn't depend on your ability to pay for it. The idea is old, and we need it more now, when information is abundant but increasingly fenced off, paywalls multiply, and algorithms decide what we see. The shelves are curated by people trained to help you find what's true, not what keeps you scrolling. A librarian will answer your question without tracking you, selling your data, or steering you toward an ad.

That winter I worked through the children's section, then the adult one, then whatever a kind librarian slid across the desk with a raised eyebrow and a "Try this." I read about places I'd never see and lives nothing like mine. I stopped feeling like the new kid. I felt like a member of something larger.

I still carry a library card, and it's one of my most prized possessions. It is proof of a bargain we made with one another, and one worth keeping: we pool our resources so that everyone, whatever their circumstances, can have access to the world.

**Museum Returns 27 Looted Artifacts to Nigeria**

A major European museum on Tuesday returned 27 looted objects to Nigeria, including ceremonial sculptures, carved ivory pieces, and bronze plaques taken during a 19th-century military expedition.

Nigerian officials received the objects at a ceremony at the museum. They had been in its African collections for more than a century, and they are expected to go on display in Lagos once conservation work is finished.

Museum director Elise Hartmann called the return "a moral responsibility and an institutional reckoning."

"These objects were acquired in circumstances that were deeply unjust," Hartmann said. "They are not simply works of art; they are part of a living cultural heritage. Returning them is the right thing to do."

The return follows years of pressure from Nigerian officials, scholars, and activists, who have argued that artifacts seized during colonial campaigns should go back to the communities they were taken from. Provenance research by the museum found that the objects were removed during a British punitive raid in 1897 and later sold through European art markets before entering its collection.

Nigeria's Minister of Culture, Amina Bello, welcomed the return, calling it "an important act of justice, dignity, and historical acknowledgment."

"For generations, these treasures were admired abroad while the people to whom they belong were denied access to them," Bello said. "Their return does not erase the past, but it helps us confront it honestly and begin to repair the damage."

Other museums in Europe and North America are also reexamining how they acquired items during the colonial period. Several have recently announced the return of bronzes, sacred objects, and human remains after evidence showed they had been taken through violence, coercion, or theft.

The issue is still contested. Some critics argue that museums serve a global public and should keep major collections, sharing them through loans and partnerships. Others say only full repatriation can correct long-standing injustices and restore cultural sovereignty.

Art historian Daniel Okoye said the latest return could encourage similar actions elsewhere. "This is not just about one museum or one set of objects," he said. "It signals a growing recognition that possession without consent cannot be justified indefinitely."

The museum said it will keep reviewing the provenance of hundreds of items in its collection and is in discussions with other countries about possible returns.

**Antikythera mechanism**

The **Antikythera mechanism** is an ancient Greek hand-powered mechanical device, often described as the earliest known analog computer. It calculated and displayed astronomical phenomena: the positions of the Sun and Moon, lunar phases, and eclipse cycles, and possibly the motions of some planets. It is usually dated to the late 2nd or early 1st century BCE.

It was found in 1901 among the remains of a shipwreck off the Greek island of Antikythera, between Crete and the Peloponnese. It survives as heavily corroded bronze fragments and drew little attention at first. Decades later, researchers found finely cut gears embedded in the fragments, and only then did the device's complexity become clear. X-ray computed tomography and other imaging techniques have since revealed much of its internal structure and inscriptions.

The mechanism sat in a wooden case about the size of a shoebox. The front face carried circular dials with pointers, probably showing the zodiac and the Egyptian calendar. A hand crank probably drove a train of more than 30 bronze gears, which turned rotation into the ratios of celestial cycles. To model the Moon's irregular motion, a pin-and-slot arrangement varied the lunar pointer's speed in a way consistent with ancient Greek astronomical theory.

The back held spiral dials for longer cycles. One showed the Metonic cycle, 19 years, which reconciles lunar months with the solar year. Another tracked the Saros cycle, used to predict eclipses. A smaller dial appears to have marked the Exeligmos, a longer eclipse cycle that improved prediction accuracy. Inscriptions on the device explained the dials and displays, much as an operating manual would.

Its precise gearing points to an established tradition of instrument-making, yet no other surviving device of comparable complexity from antiquity is known. Scholars have linked it to Greek scientific traditions associated with Hipparchus, Posidonius, and Archimedes. Its exact origin and maker remain uncertain. What it does show is that Greek craftsmen and astronomers could build advanced mathematical knowledge into a working machine.

**A City Center Without Cars**

The first time I stood in a city center with no cars, I heard it before I understood it: a busker's out-of-tune accordion, a toddler shrieking with joy at a pigeon, two old men arguing over chess. About a minute passed before I worked out what was missing. It was the low, constant growl I had always taken for silence.

That was in a mid-sized European city, on a trip I'd taken mostly to get away from my own. At home I drive everywhere, and I'm not proud of it. My downtown is a place I put up with. I circle for parking, pay too much for it, then walk half a mile past gray garages. So when people propose banning cars from city centers, I get defensive. What about my groceries? My mother, who can't walk far? The plumber, the ambulance, the delivery driver?

Those questions deserve real answers, and the best car-free centers have them. Ambulances and fire trucks get through. Residents with disabilities get permits and drop-off zones. Deliveries happen in early-morning windows. Done well, a ban works more like a filter than a wall. The busiest, most valuable square mile of a city shouldn't be organized around the least efficient way to move people through it.

And it is inefficient. A single lane of car traffic moves maybe 2,000 people an hour, while the same width given to a tram or to pedestrians moves many times that. We spend enormous amounts of prime real estate storing empty vehicles, then wonder why rents are high and public space is scarce.

I still don't think the answer is a flat yes. I've seen bans imposed on cities that offered nothing in return: no reliable buses, no safe bike lanes, no affordable alternative. There, a ban doesn't produce a lively plaza. It punishes the shift worker who commutes from the outskirts at midnight, after the trains have stopped. Cities that ban first and build later are mostly running an experiment on their poorest residents.

My view is conditional but firm. Cities should move toward car-free centers, and they should earn it by building the alternatives first, or at least at the same time. Make the train faster than the drive. Make the bike lane feel safe to an eleven-year-old. Then close the street, and people will barely argue.

I changed my mind watching that European square at dusk. The chess players packed up, families took their place, and children wove between café tables without a parent's hand clamped to their shoulder. Nobody seemed to be in a hurry or in danger. I had never seen a city center behave like a living room before.

I still drive at home, but I've started parking at the edge of downtown and walking in. The first few times, it felt like a loss. Now it feels like a rehearsal for a city whose center belongs to the people in it.

# Artemisia Gentileschi

**Artemisia Gentileschi** (8 July 1593 – c. 1656) was an Italian Baroque painter who worked in the tradition of Caravaggio. Her compositions are dramatic and naturalistic, and she often painted women from myth, scripture, and history. She was the first woman admitted to the Accademia delle Arti del Disegno in Florence.

## Early life

Artemisia was born in Rome, the eldest child of the painter Orazio Gentileschi and Prudentia Montone. Her mother died when she was about twelve. She trained in her father's workshop, where she learned drawing, color mixing, and painting techniques. Women were barred from formal academies, so her education stayed in the studio. Her earliest signed work, *Susanna and the Elders* (1610), was painted when she was seventeen.

## Trial of Agostino Tassi

In 1611, Agostino Tassi raped her. He was a painter and a colleague of her father, hired to teach her perspective. Orazio brought charges in 1612, and the trial lasted seven months. Artemisia was reportedly examined under torture with thumbscrews to verify her testimony. Tassi was convicted, but his sentence of exile from Rome was not enforced for long. The surviving transcripts record a woman's testimony, which is rare for this period.

## Career

Shortly after the trial, Artemisia married the Florentine artist Pierantonio Stiattesi and moved to Florence. There she won the patronage of Cosimo II de' Medici and became friends with Galileo Galilei. In 1616 she joined the Accademia delle Arti del Disegno. Her works from these years include *Judith Slaying Holofernes* (c. 1614–20) and *Self-Portrait as a Lute Player*.

Debts drove her back to Rome in the 1620s, and she later worked in Venice and Naples. In 1638 she joined her father at the court of Charles I in England, and after Orazio's death in 1639 she completed some of his commissions. Most of her later career was spent in Naples, where she collaborated with other painters and received prominent commissions.

## Style and themes

Gentileschi's paintings use strong chiaroscuro, vivid color, and emotional intensity. She frequently depicted Judith, Susanna, Esther, Bathsheba, and Cleopatra. Her heroines are physically strong and psychologically complex, unlike the more passive women common in the work of her male contemporaries.

## Legacy

After her death, Gentileschi was largely overlooked for centuries. Art historians, notably feminist scholars, rediscovered her work in the 20th century and reassessed her significance. Her life and art have since inspired books, plays, and films. Major exhibitions have followed, including one at the National Gallery, London, in 2020.

# Migration Guide: Config Format v1 → v2

Version 2 changes how the config file is structured, renames several fields, and requires native types for booleans and numbers. This guide lists the breaking changes and shows how to convert a v1 file.

## Summary of Breaking Changes

1. Root-level keys are now grouped into sections.
2. Several fields have new names.
3. Booleans and numbers must be real YAML/JSON types, not strings.
4. Environment-specific overrides now live in an `environments` block.
5. Deprecated v1 fields are no longer supported.

## Key Changes

### 1. Top-level structure

In v1, most settings sat at the root. In v2 they are grouped under:

- `server`
- `logging`
- `auth`
- `environments`

### 2. Renamed fields

The main renames:

- `host` → `server.host`
- `port` → `server.port`
- `logLevel` → `logging.level`
- `logFile` → `logging.file`
- `enableAuth` → `auth.enabled`

### 3. Strict value types

v1 often accepted strings such as `"true"` or `"8080"`. v2 requires native types:

- `"true"` → `true`
- `"8080"` → `8080`

### 4. Environment overrides

v1 used flattened keys such as `dev_host` or `prod_port`. In v2, these go under:

```yaml
environments:
  dev:
    server:
      host: ...
  prod:
    server:
      port: ...
```

## Example Migration

### v1

```yaml
host: "localhost"
port: "8080"
logLevel: "debug"
logFile: "/var/log/app.log"
enableAuth: "true"
dev_host: "dev.local"
prod_host: "prod.example.com"
```

### v2

```yaml
server:
  host: localhost
  port: 8080

logging:
  level: debug
  file: /var/log/app.log

auth:
  enabled: true

environments:
  dev:
    server:
      host: dev.local
  prod:
    server:
      host: prod.example.com
```

## Removed Fields

v2 does not support these v1 fields:

- `timeoutMs`: replaced by `server.timeout`, which is in seconds
- `authModeLegacy`: removed; use `auth.provider`
- `debug`: replaced by `logging.level: debug`

## Migration Tips

- Validate the file against the v2 schema before you deploy.
- Update any scripts that read the old field names.
- Quoted booleans and numbers now fail validation, so look for them.
- Try the migration in a staging environment first, one change at a time.

## Checklist

- [ ] Nest root settings under the right sections
- [ ] Rename deprecated keys
- [ ] Convert stringified booleans and numbers to native types
- [ ] Move environment-specific values into `environments`
- [ ] Remove unsupported legacy fields

# photodate

`photodate` renames photos by the date they were taken. It reads the EXIF capture date and names each file in a sortable format such as `2024-07-14_15-32-08.jpg`.

## Features

- Reads the original capture date from EXIF data
- Uses the file's modified time when EXIF is missing
- Filename templates you can change
- Dry-run mode to preview changes
- Adds a counter when two photos share a timestamp
- Undoes the most recent run
- Supports JPEG, HEIC, PNG, TIFF, and common RAW formats

## Installation

With pip:

```bash
pip install photodate
```

Or from source:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/example/photodate.git
cd photodate
pip install .
```

Requires Python 3.9 or newer.

## Usage

```bash
photodate [OPTIONS] PATH...
```

`PATH` can be one or more files or directories.

### Quick start

Preview what would change:

```bash
photodate --dry-run ~/Pictures/vacation
```

Rename for real:

```bash
photodate ~/Pictures/vacation
```

Include subfolders:

```bash
photodate --recursive ~/Pictures
```

## Options

| Option | Description |
|---|---|
| `-n`, `--dry-run` | Show planned renames without changing anything |
| `-r`, `--recursive` | Process directories recursively |
| `-f`, `--format TEMPLATE` | Filename template (default: `%Y-%m-%d_%H-%M-%S`) |
| `--fallback [mtime\|skip]` | What to do when EXIF is missing (default: `mtime`) |
| `--prefix TEXT` | Add a prefix to every filename |
| `--lowercase-ext` | Convert file extensions to lowercase |
| `--undo` | Revert the last run |
| `-v`, `--verbose` | Print every rename |

## Templates

Templates use standard `strftime` codes:

```bash
photodate --format "%Y/%m/IMG_%Y%m%d_%H%M%S" photos/
```

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `%Y` | Four-digit year |
| `%m` | Month (01–12) |
| `%d` | Day of month |
| `%H` `%M` `%S` | Hour, minute, second |

## Duplicate timestamps

Burst shots often share a timestamp. When two names collide, `photodate` appends a counter:

```
2024-07-14_15-32-08.jpg
2024-07-14_15-32-08_2.jpg
2024-07-14_15-32-08_3.jpg
```

Existing files are never overwritten.

## Undo

Each run writes a log to `~/.photodate/last_run.json`. To revert:

```bash
photodate --undo
```

Only the most recent run can be undone.

## Contributing

Bug reports and pull requests are welcome. Please run `pytest` before submitting changes.

## License

MIT

# photodate

`photodate` renames photos by the date they were taken. It reads the EXIF capture date and names each file in a sortable format such as `2024-07-14_15-32-08.jpg`.

## Features

- Reads the original capture date from EXIF data
- Uses the file's modified time when EXIF is missing
- Filename templates you can change
- Dry-run mode to preview changes
- Adds a counter when two photos share a timestamp
- Undoes the most recent run
- Works on JPEG, HEIC, PNG, TIFF, and common RAW formats

## Installation

With pip:

```bash
pip install photodate
```

Or from source:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/example/photodate.git
cd photodate
pip install .
```

Requires Python 3.9 or newer.

## Usage

```bash
photodate [OPTIONS] PATH...
```

`PATH` can be one or more files or directories.

Preview what would change:

```bash
photodate --dry-run ~/Pictures/vacation
```

Rename for real:

```bash
photodate ~/Pictures/vacation
```

Include subfolders:

```bash
photodate --recursive ~/Pictures
```

## Options

- `-n`, `--dry-run`: show planned renames without changing anything
- `-r`, `--recursive`: process directories recursively
- `-f`, `--format TEMPLATE`: filename template (default: `%Y-%m-%d_%H-%M-%S`)
- `--fallback [mtime|skip]`: what to do when EXIF is missing (default: `mtime`)
- `--prefix TEXT`: add a prefix to every filename
- `--lowercase-ext`: convert file extensions to lowercase
- `--undo`: revert the last run
- `-v`, `--verbose`: print every rename

## Templates

Templates use standard `strftime` codes:

```bash
photodate --format "%Y/%m/IMG_%Y%m%d_%H%M%S" photos/
```

- `%m`: month (01–12)

# Hartwell Museum Returns 27 Looted Artifacts to Nigeria

**Benin bronzes and ceremonial objects will go on display in Benin City after more than a century abroad**

*Hartwell, England* — A regional museum in northern England formally returned 27 artifacts to Nigeria on Tuesday, ending a decade of negotiations. British forces took the objects during a colonial-era military expedition in 1897.

The Hartwell Museum of World Cultures transferred legal ownership of the collection to Nigeria's National Commission for Museums and Monuments at a ceremony attended by diplomats, museum staff, and members of the Edo diaspora community. The items include brass plaques, carved ivory pieces, and a ceremonial staff that once belonged to the royal court of the Kingdom of Benin.

"These are not simply objects," said Dr. Amara Okonkwo, the Nigerian delegation's lead representative. "They are records of our history, our artistry, and our identity. For generations, our communities have studied these works through photographs in foreign books. Today, that changes."

In 1897, British forces attacked Benin City and removed thousands of items from the royal palace. Many were sold at auction or passed to private collectors and institutions across Europe and North America. The museum acquired its pieces in 1934 through a bequest from the family of a former naval officer.

Museum director Helen Marsh said the decision followed extensive provenance research, which confirmed where the objects came from. "We had to ask ourselves what responsibility we have when we know how an object came to us," Marsh said. "The answer, ultimately, was clear. Holding onto them was no longer defensible."

Other institutions have made similar returns. In recent years, museums in Germany, the United States, and Scotland have returned portions of their Benin collections, while the British Museum continues to face calls for restitution of its much larger holdings.

Some curators argue that universal museums allow global audiences to encounter diverse cultures. Others have raised concerns about conservation capacity, though supporters of restitution note that Nigeria is building the Edo Museum of West African Art, designed by architect David Adjaye, to house returned works.

Chidi Eze, a London-based university student of Edo descent, attended the ceremony. "My grandmother used to tell me stories about the palace and the bronzes," he said. "I never thought I would see any of this come home in my lifetime."

The artifacts will be flown to Lagos next week and then taken to Benin City, where they are expected to go on public display by early next year.

Boredom gets treated as a minor curse, something to avoid as urgently as hunger or loneliness. A boring class, a boring conversation, a boring afternoon: each feels like a design flaw, proof that life is not entertaining us the way it should. For a long time I agreed. Waiting in line, sitting on a bus, staring at the ceiling with nothing to do, I reached for my phone almost without deciding to. Every empty stretch of the day was a problem, and the phone solved it. Later I came to see that boredom can be an opening.

As a child I met it on summer afternoons, when the heat was too heavy for running outside, the television had nothing I wanted, and my friends were away. At first it was unbearable. I paced from room to room telling anyone who would listen that there was "nothing to do." Then the complaint wore itself out, and I would start building strange worlds from ordinary things. Blankets became forts. Notebooks became newspapers for imaginary cities. A box of mismatched buttons became treasure. I had to get through the boredom before imagination could start.

The pattern did not disappear as I grew older. It got harder to see. Adults have endless ways out of boredom, many of them glowing in the palm of the hand, and the moment a task turns repetitive or a silence stretches, a distraction is there. But constant stimulation leaves me feeling thin, as though my attention had been broken into pieces that cannot settle anywhere. Boredom gathers me back together. It slows time enough for thoughts I have been avoiding, or have been too busy to hear, to come up.

Some of my clearest ideas have come at dull moments: folding laundry, walking a familiar route, sitting through the first uneventful minutes of a delayed train. My mind wanders there, and wandering is often where reflection begins. Boredom takes the urgency away and leaves a slower kind of attention, less efficient and roomier. Memory and curiosity get a turn, and so does discomfort. Without it, I suspect I would know less about what I think.

Boredom also reminds me that not every moment exists for my amusement. The world owes me no constant novelty. Sitting still in a waiting room, listening through a quiet pause, letting an afternoon unfold without demanding anything from it: that is patience, and it takes some humility. A meaningful life has thrilling scenes in it, but most of it is ordinary stretches that call for endurance and a little invention.

I still dislike boredom sometimes, and I still reach for distraction more often than I mean to. But I no longer see it as a void to fill as quickly as possible. I see it as an interval where something quieter can surface. In a culture that fears silence and worships stimulation, it may be one of the few places left where the mind can hear itself think.

# Contributing Guide

This is an open-source documentation site, and we take contributions of any size: a typo fix, a clearer explanation, new content, or a change to how pages are organized.

## Ways to Contribute

- Fix spelling, grammar, or formatting
- Clarify an existing explanation
- Add examples, tutorials, or reference material
- Report outdated or incorrect information
- Improve accessibility and readability
- Suggest better navigation or organization

Not sure your idea fits? Open an issue and ask.

## Before You Start

- Read a few existing pages to get the style and structure
- Search open issues and pull requests so you do not duplicate work
- Check whether the change is already under discussion

For larger changes, open an issue before you write anything. We can agree on the scope first, which saves time on both sides.

## Getting Started

1. Fork the repository
2. Create a new branch for your changes
3. Make your edits
4. Preview the site locally if you can
5. Commit with a clear message
6. Open a pull request

Name the branch for what it does, like `fix-installation-typo` or `add-api-auth-guide`.

## Writing Guidelines

- Write in clear, direct language and avoid unnecessary jargon
- Keep paragraphs short and headings descriptive
- Prefer examples to abstract explanations
- Use the same terms across pages
- Link to related pages where they help

Make sure technical examples are accurate and easy to follow. Test any command or code snippet when you can.

## Style and Formatting

Follow the project's conventions for:

- Markdown structure and heading levels
- Code block formatting with language tags
- File naming
- Internal linking

If the repository has linting or formatting tools, run them before you submit your pull request.

## Pull Request Expectations

A good pull request:

- Explains what changed and why
- Stays on a single topic when possible
- Includes screenshots or previews for visual changes

Expect feedback. Review is a normal part of the process.

## Reporting Issues

If you find a problem but do not want to fix it yourself, open an issue. Include:

- A clear title
- A link to the affected page
- A description of the problem
- A suggested fix, if you have one

## Code of Conduct

Be respectful and constructive. We want the project to be welcoming to contributors at every experience level.

Talk about the decline of letter writing usually starts with nostalgia: envelopes, stamps, the small thrill of recognizing a handwriting before you read a word. That feeling is real. But the loss goes deeper than a charming old habit. When we stop writing letters, we give up a way of thinking and a way of paying attention to each other.

A letter asks more of us than a text or an email does. It asks us to sit still until we find out what we want to say. Most modern messages are built for speed. We reply fast, revise where nobody sees, send half a thought, and fill a silence before it has a chance to deepen. A letter moves at the pace of reflection. It takes time to write, seal, send, and receive, and that delay makes the writer more deliberate and less impulsive. Few people spend a letter on their lunch or a passing irritation. You gather yourself and put your experience into words, and afterward you often understand your own mind better.

I think this is among the quietest losses. Without letters we lose a private workshop for the self. A letter is not quite a conversation and not quite a diary; it sits between them. It is personal, yet addressed to one particular person rather than to the void, and that reader matters. In letters we tend to be a little more thoughtful and more willing to explain what we mean. Writing to someone we love can refine our character as well as our sentences.

Letters also keep feeling in a way instant messages rarely do. A text can say “I miss you.” A letter shows that someone made it by hand: the pressure of the pen, the slant of the lines, the crossings-out, the margin added as an afterthought. These details are traces of a living moment. A letter is language, but it is also an object, and it travels through weather and distance. You can fold it into a drawer and open it years later, and it brings back a lost version of the person who wrote it. Holding an old letter, you meet what someone felt and also how they moved through time.

Letters teach us to wait, and without them we grow less patient with absence. The waiting is not empty. It gives longing room to turn into attention. Now that we can reach anyone instantly, we expect access and mistake it for presence, and we take constant contact for closeness. Closeness does not always grow from frequency. Sometimes it grows from concentration, from choosing words carefully, from speaking across a silence instead of erasing it.

I do not think we have to reject new forms of communication to mourn what letters gave us. Texts, emails, and calls all have their uses. Letters offered something else: a durable record of thought shaped by time and care. Losing them costs us an art and a human tempo, one of the few ways of communicating that asks us to slow down enough to mean what we say.

To hold an old letter is to encounter not only what someone felt, but how they moved through time.

Letters teach us to wait, and without them we grow less patient with absence. The waiting is not empty. It gives longing room to turn into attention. Now that we can reach anyone instantly, we expect access and mistake it for presence, and we take constant contact for closeness. But closeness does not always grow from frequency. Sometimes it grows from concentration, from choosing words carefully, from speaking across a silence instead of erasing it.

I do not think we have to reject new forms of communication to mourn what letters gave us. Texts have their uses, emails are efficient, calls are immediate. But letters offered something these forms seldom do: a durable record of thought shaped by time and care. When we stop writing letters, we lose not only an art, but a human tempo, one of the few ways of communicating that asks us to slow down enough to mean what we say.

# Migrating Configuration Files from v1 to v2

This guide covers the changes between v1 and v2 of the configuration format and how to update your files. Examples use YAML.

## Summary of Changes

| Area | v1 | v2 |
|---|---|---|
| Version field | Optional | **Required** (`version: 2`) |
| Server settings | Flat keys | Nested under `server` |
| Timeouts | Integers (seconds) | Duration strings (`"30s"`) |
| Environment variables | `$VAR` | `${VAR}` or `${VAR:-default}` |
| Booleans | `yes`/`no` accepted | `true`/`false` only |
| `log_file` | Supported | Removed; use `logging.output` |

## Step 1: Add the Version Field

Add this at the top of every file. v2 parsers reject files without it.

```yaml
version: 2
```

## Step 2: Nest Server Settings

The flat `host`, `port`, and `timeout` keys now live under `server`.

**v1**
```yaml
host: 0.0.0.0
port: 8080
timeout: 30
```

**v2**
```yaml
server:
  host: 0.0.0.0
  port: 8080
  timeout: "30s"
```

## Step 3: Convert Timeouts to Durations

All time values must be strings with a unit: `ms`, `s`, `m`, or `h`. Bare integers now raise a validation error because the old implicit unit (seconds) caused confusion.

## Step 4: Update Environment Variable Syntax

Change `$DB_PASSWORD` to `${DB_PASSWORD}`. You can now supply fallbacks:

```yaml
database:
  password: ${DB_PASSWORD:-changeme}
```

Literal dollar signs must be escaped as `$$`.

## Step 5: Replace Deprecated Options

`log_file` is removed. Use the `logging` block instead:

**v1**
```yaml
log_file: /var/log/app.log
```

**v2**
```yaml
logging:
  output: /var/log/app.log
  level: info
```

## Step 6: Fix Boolean Values

Replace `yes`, `no`, `on`, and `off` with `true` or `false`. v2 follows YAML 1.2, which no longer treats the older forms as booleans.

## Automated Migration

A converter handles most of these changes:

```bash
config-tool migrate --from 1 --to 2 config.yaml -o config.v2.yaml
```

Review the output before deploying. The tool cannot infer the right `logging.level`, so it defaults to `info`.

## Validating the Result

```bash
config-tool validate config.v2.yaml
```

Fix any reported errors, which include line numbers.

## Rollback

Keep your v1 files until v2 has run successfully in production. v1 files remain readable by v1-compatible releases, but v2 files are not backward compatible.

## Common Pitfalls

- **Unquoted durations:** `30s` works, but `30` fails.
- **Unescaped `$`:** Passwords containing `$` may be misread as variables.
- **Mixed versions:** Included files must all use the same version.

# Atacama Desert

The **Atacama Desert** (Spanish: *Desierto de Atacama*) is a desert plateau on the Pacific coast of western South America, covering a strip of land roughly 1,600 km (1,000 mi) long, mostly in northern Chile. It is widely regarded as the driest non-polar desert in the world and is one of the oldest continuously arid regions on Earth.

## Geography

The desert lies between the Pacific Ocean and the Andes Mountains, extending from the southern border of Peru to around La Serena in Chile. It covers approximately 105,000 km² (41,000 sq mi), though broader definitions that include adjacent arid regions give a larger area. The terrain includes salt flats (*salares*), sand dunes, rocky plains, and volcanic peaks. The Salar de Atacama, the largest salt flat in Chile, lies in the east of the region.

## Climate

The extreme aridity has several causes. The Andes block moisture from the Amazon Basin to the east, while the cold Humboldt Current and a persistent subtropical high-pressure system suppress rainfall from the Pacific. Some weather stations in the interior have never recorded rainfall, and the average annual precipitation in many areas is under 15 mm (0.6 in). Some parts of the desert appear to have been hyperarid for millions of years.

Despite the dryness, coastal areas experience a persistent fog known as *camanchaca*, which provides moisture for some plant and animal life.

## Ecology

Vegetation is sparse, but the desert supports specialized organisms, including cacti, lichens, and hardy shrubs. In rare years of heavy rainfall, often linked to El Niño, parts of the desert bloom in a phenomenon called *desierto florido* ("flowering desert"). Fauna includes vicuñas, guanacos, foxes, flamingos in the salt lakes, and reptiles and insects. Researchers have also studied microbial life in the soils, which are sometimes compared to those of Mars.

## History and economy

Indigenous peoples, including the Atacameño (Lickanantay) and Chinchorro cultures, inhabited the region for thousands of years. In the 19th century, the desert became economically important for its deposits of nitrate (saltpeter) and guano, which were used to make fertilizer. Control over these resources contributed to the War of the Pacific (1879–1884), in which Chile gained territory from Bolivia and Peru.

Today, mining dominates the economy, particularly copper and lithium. The Chuquicamata mine is among the largest open-pit copper mines in the world.

## Astronomy and science

The desert's high altitude, dry air, and minimal light pollution make it well suited to astronomical observation. Facilities include the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) and the Paranal Observatory, which houses the Very Large Telescope.

## Tourism

Popular destinations include San Pedro de Atacama, the Valle de la Luna, the El Tatio geysers, and several high-altitude lagoons.

# The Slow Arithmetic of Walking

I never meant to become a person who walks. My car was in the shop for a week, and the bus to my office needed a transfer that added forty minutes. So one gray Tuesday I left the house on foot, grumbling, with no plan beyond figuring something out.

Around the third mile I noticed I hadn't been alone with my thoughts in years.

Walking is too slow to count as getting somewhere and too fast to count as standing still. Your body is busy and your mind wanders off. Problems I had been clenching my jaw over for weeks loosened on their own. I'd turn a corner and know how to word the difficult email, or realize I'd been angry at my brother for the wrong reason. Nietzsche claimed that all truly great thoughts are conceived while walking. I can't speak to the great ones, but the useful ones show up that way for me.

When the car came back, I kept walking. Mornings, mostly, before the day made its demands. I started to know my neighborhood the way you know a person, not a map. One man watered his tomatoes in a faded bathrobe and raised a single finger as I passed, like a conductor cueing one violin. On one corner the smell of baking bread drifted out of a vent at exactly 6:40. A persimmon tree I had passed a hundred times turned out to be heavy with fruit, bright as lanterns against the bare branches. I wondered how much else I'd driven past.

Some days it rains and I go anyway. Those are often the best, with the streets rinsed and empty and my footsteps keeping time. Some days I'm tired or sad and the walk fixes nothing, but I get to carry the sadness at three miles an hour, which is easier.

A mile is about two thousand steps, and a good walk is a few thousand more. No single step feels like an accomplishment, and nobody applauds one. But they add up, like pennies in a jar, to a year of mornings and a body that is stronger than it was.

Much of modern life is built to spare us effort, and it spares us experience along with it. Walking costs time. What I get back is the texture of a place and the odd peace of being exactly as fast as I am.

Tomorrow morning I'll lace up my shoes again. I don't know what I'll think about.

# Battle of Hastings

The **Battle of Hastings** was fought on 14 October 1066 between the Norman-French army of William, Duke of Normandy, and an English army under the Anglo-Saxon King Harold Godwinson. It took place about 7 miles (11 km) northwest of Hastings, close to the present-day town of Battle, East Sussex. The battle was a decisive Norman victory and began the Norman Conquest of England.

## Background

In January 1066, the childless King Edward the Confessor died, triggering a succession crisis. Harold Godwinson, the powerful Earl of Wessex, was crowned king almost immediately. However, William of Normandy claimed that Edward had promised him the throne and that Harold had sworn an oath to support his claim. Meanwhile, the Norwegian king Harald Hardrada also pressed a claim, invading northern England in September 1066.

Harold marched north and defeated Hardrada at the Battle of Stamford Bridge on 25 September. Only days later, William's invasion fleet landed at Pevensey on the Sussex coast on 28 September. Harold hurried his army south, covering roughly 250 miles in about two weeks.

## Battle

Harold's forces took up a defensive position on Senlac Hill, forming a shield wall along the ridge. The English army consisted largely of infantry, including elite housecarls and the less-equipped fyrd. William's army included infantry, archers, crossbowmen, and a significant cavalry contingent.

The fighting began in the morning, with Norman archers firing uphill with limited effect. Infantry and cavalry assaults followed but failed to break the shield wall. At one point, a rumour spread that William had been killed, and he reportedly lifted his helmet to show he was alive. Some Norman troops retreated, and some English soldiers pursued them down the hill, only to be cut down when the Normans turned on them. Whether the Normans used feigned retreats deliberately remains debated among historians.

As the day wore on, the English line weakened. Harold was killed late in the day, traditionally said to have been struck in the eye by an arrow, as depicted in the Bayeux Tapestry, although this is disputed. With their king dead, the English forces broke and fled.

## Aftermath

William continued to consolidate his position, receiving submission from English leaders and being crowned King of England on 25 December 1066 at Westminster Abbey. He later founded Battle Abbey on the site of the battle. The conquest changed English society, language, law, and landholding.

## See also

- Norman Conquest
- Bayeux Tapestry
- Battle of Stamford Bridge

It took place about 7 miles (11 km) northwest of Hastings, close to the present-day town of Battle, East Sussex. The battle was a decisive Norman victory and began the Norman Conquest of England.

## Background

In January 1066, the childless King Edward the Confessor died, triggering a succession crisis. Harold Godwinson, the powerful Earl of Wessex, was crowned king almost immediately. However, William of Normandy claimed that Edward had promised him the throne and that Harold had sworn an oath to support his claim. Meanwhile, the Norwegian king Harald Hardrada also pressed a claim, invading northern England in September 1066.

Harold marched north and defeated Hardrada at the Battle of Stamford Bridge on 25 September. Only days later, William's invasion fleet landed at Pevensey on the Sussex coast on 28 September. Harold hurried his army south, covering roughly 250 miles in about two weeks.

## Battle

Harold's forces took up a defensive position on Senlac Hill, forming a shield wall along the ridge. The English army consisted largely of infantry, including elite housecarls and the less-equipped fyrd. William's army included infantry, archers, crossbowmen, and a significant cavalry contingent.

The fighting began in the morning, with Norman archers firing uphill with limited effect. Infantry and cavalry assaults followed but failed to break the shield wall. At one point, a rumour spread that William had been killed, and he reportedly lifted his helmet to show he was alive. Some Norman troops retreated, and some English soldiers pursued them down the hill, only to be cut down when the Normans turned on them. Whether the Normans used feigned retreats deliberately remains debated among historians.

As the day wore on, the English line weakened. Harold was killed late in the day, traditionally said to have been struck in the eye by an arrow, as depicted in the Bayeux Tapestry, although this is disputed. With their king dead, the English forces broke and fled.

## Aftermath

William continued to consolidate his position, receiving submission from English leaders and being crowned King of England on 25 December 1066 at Westminster Abbey. He later founded Battle Abbey on the site of the battle. The conquest changed English society, language, law, and landholding.

## See also

- Norman Conquest
- Bayeux Tapestry
- Battle of Stamford Bridge

**Transit workers strike, halting most city buses, subways and trams**

Thousands of commuters were stuck with long delays Tuesday after public-transit workers walked off the job, halting most bus, subway, and tram service across the city.

The strike began shortly after midnight. The Transit Workers Union and the Metropolitan Transit Authority had spent weeks in contract talks without reaching a deal. Union leaders say workers want higher wages, stronger job protections, and better staffing. They argue that employees have worked under growing pressure for years, with living costs rising and too few people on the job.

"This strike is a last resort," said union president Maria Delgado at an early morning rally outside the transit authority's headquarters. "Our members keep this city moving every day, but they are being asked to do more with less. We need a contract that reflects the value of their work and guarantees safe, reliable service for the public."

Transit officials said they were disappointed by the walkout and warned that a strike lasting several days could badly hurt the economy. In a statement, the authority said it had offered a "fair and responsible" contract package with pay increases and benefit protections. It said the union's demands would put an unsustainable burden on a budget that is already strained.

"We remain committed to reaching an agreement as quickly as possible," said transit authority chief executive Daniel Mercer. "We urge union leadership to return to the bargaining table so we can restore service for the millions who depend on public transportation."

By dawn, commuters were crowding rideshare pick-up zones and the limited regional rail service, and lining up at bike-share stations. Downtown streets were heavily congested as more residents drove, took taxis, or carpooled. Several schools reported higher-than-usual absences. Some businesses said employees were arriving late or working remotely where they could.

City officials urged residents to avoid nonessential travel. They announced expanded bike lanes, additional traffic officers at major intersections, and more commuter-rail capacity. The mayor's office said it was watching the situation closely and encouraged both sides to resume talks with the help of a state-appointed mediator.

Commuter Jasmine Lee spent nearly two hours trying to reach her office. "I understand why workers are upset, but this is chaos," she said. "So many people rely on these trains and buses. I just hope they settle this soon."

Negotiations were expected to continue Tuesday afternoon. Neither side said how close they were to a deal.

Artemisia Gentileschi (1593 – c. 1656) was an Italian Baroque painter. She was among the first women to succeed professionally in a field then dominated by men. Her best-known subjects are biblical and mythological heroines.

She was born in Rome, the daughter of the painter Orazio Gentileschi, who gave her her earliest training. Caravaggio influenced her style, in particular his dramatic light and shadow and his naturalism. Women had limited access to artistic education at the time, but she was already skilled when young. *Susanna and the Elders* (1610), one of her earliest known works, conveys psychological tension and female experience.

In 1612 the painter Agostino Tassi, who had raped her, stood trial. Artemisia was subjected to public scrutiny and to torture meant to verify her testimony. Modern readings of her life and art often start from this trial. Soon afterward she married the Florentine painter Pierantonio Stiattesi and moved to Florence, where she established her career. In 1616 she became the first woman admitted to the Accademia delle Arti del Disegno.

She painted many of her best-known works in Florence and later in Rome, Venice, and Naples, among them *Judith Slaying Holofernes*, *Judith and Her Maidservant*, *Lucretia*, and *Self-Portrait as the Allegory of Painting*. Her subjects are often women from history, scripture, and legend at a moment of crisis, courage, or revenge. Other Baroque artists painted such subjects too. Hers are noted for their intensity and emotional complexity.

She worked for elite patrons across Italy and beyond. Naples became the center of her later career. She probably traveled to London in the late 1630s to join her father at the court of Charles I of England, and may have worked on court commissions there before returning to Naples.

After her death she was overshadowed by her male contemporaries and was often remembered mainly through her biography. Her reputation has grown since the twentieth century. Scholars have praised her technique and her originality within Baroque painting, and she is now ranked among the leading painters of her age.

# VoltHaus Recalls 42,000 Home Batteries Over Overheating Risk

**Austin-based startup says it has received 31 reports of overheating, including 6 small fires; no injuries reported**

AUSTIN, Texas — VoltHaus, a home energy startup, announced Tuesday a voluntary recall of about 42,000 of its HearthCell 10 residential battery units after discovering a defect that can cause the devices to overheat and, in rare cases, catch fire.

The recall covers units manufactured between March 2022 and August 2023 and sold in the United States and Canada. The company said it has received 31 reports of overheating worldwide, including six incidents in which the unit smoldered or ignited. No injuries have been reported, though two homeowners reported minor property damage to garage walls.

According to VoltHaus, the problem stems from a flaw in a batch of internal wiring connectors supplied by a third-party manufacturer. Under certain conditions, such as repeated rapid charging in high ambient temperatures, the connectors can degrade and create resistance that generates excess heat.

"Safety is the foundation of everything we build, and we fell short here," said Dana Okafor, VoltHaus co-founder and chief executive, in a statement. "We are contacting every affected customer directly, and we will repair or replace every unit at no cost."

The HearthCell 10, which retails for about $8,900 installed, stores solar energy for use at night or during power outages. VoltHaus says it has sold roughly 60,000 units since launching in 2021, so the recall covers most of its installed base.

Customers can check whether their unit is affected by entering the serial number, found on a label on the unit's right side, at the company's recall website. VoltHaus is advising owners of affected units to switch the battery to "limited mode" through its mobile app, which caps charging speed and reduces heat buildup until a technician can complete the repair. Owners who cannot access the app are urged to call the company's dedicated hotline.

The company said technicians will replace the connectors in a process that takes about two hours. Repairs are expected to begin next week, with priority given to homes where batteries are installed inside attached garages or living spaces.

Analysts say the recall could strain the young company's finances. VoltHaus raised $120 million in a funding round last year and has been preparing for a public offering. "A recall of this size is expensive, but the bigger risk is reputational," said Marcus Lindqvist, an energy storage analyst at Brightline Research. "How they handle the next few weeks will matter more than the defect itself."

The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission is reviewing the recall, a spokesperson said.

# csvkit-lite

A small, dependency-free Python library for parsing CSV files with type inference, header handling, and streaming support.

## Requirements

- Python 3.8 or newer
- No third-party dependencies

## Installation

Install from PyPI using pip:

```bash
pip install csvkit-lite
```

To install the latest development version directly from GitHub:

```bash
pip install git+https://github.com/example/csvkit-lite.git
```

For an isolated setup, use a virtual environment:

```bash
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate    # On Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install csvkit-lite
```

Verify the installation:

```bash
python -c "import csvkit_lite; print(csvkit_lite.__version__)"
```

## Quick Start

Suppose you have a file called `people.csv`:

```csv
name,age,city
Alice,34,Boston
Bob,28,Denver
Carol,41,Austin
```

### Reading rows as dictionaries

```python
from csvkit_lite import read_csv

for row in read_csv("people.csv"):
    print(row["name"], row["age"])
```

By default, the first line is treated as a header, and each row is returned as a dictionary.

### Automatic type conversion

Enable type inference to convert numbers and booleans automatically:

```python
rows = list(read_csv("people.csv", infer_types=True))
print(rows[0]["age"] + 1)   # 35, since age is an int
```

### Custom delimiters and headers

Use the `delimiter` option for tab-separated or semicolon-separated files. If your file has no header row, supply column names yourself:

```python
rows = read_csv(
    "data.tsv",
    delimiter="\t",
    header=False,
    columns=["id", "score", "label"],
)
```

### Streaming large files

`read_csv` returns a generator, so rows are read lazily and memory usage stays low even for large files:

```python
total = 0
for row in read_csv("huge.csv", infer_types=True):
    total += row["amount"]
print(total)
```

### Loading everything at once

If you prefer a simple list, wrap the call:

```python
data = list(read_csv("people.csv"))
```

## Handling Errors

Malformed rows raise a `CSVParseError` that includes the line number:

```python
from csvkit_lite import read_csv, CSVParseError

try:
    rows = list(read_csv("broken.csv"))
except CSVParseError as err:
    print(f"Problem on line {err.line}: {err}")
```

Pass `skip_errors=True` to ignore bad rows instead.

## Next Steps

- Run the tests with `pytest`
- Read the full API reference in the `docs/` folder
- Report bugs on the GitHub issue tracker

# csvkit-lite

A small, dependency-free Python library for parsing CSV files with type inference, header handling, and streaming support.

## Requirements

- Python 3.8 or newer
- No third-party dependencies

## Installation

Install from PyPI using pip:

```bash
pip install csvkit-lite
```

To install the latest development version directly from GitHub:

```bash
pip install git+https://github.com/example/csvkit-lite.git
```

For an isolated setup, use a virtual environment:

```bash
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate    # On Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install csvkit-lite
```

Verify the installation:

```bash
python -c "import csvkit_lite; print(csvkit_lite.__version__)"
```

## Quick Start

Suppose you have a file called `people.csv`:

```csv
name,age,city
Alice,34,Boston
Bob,28,Denver
Carol,41,Austin
```

## Reading rows as dictionaries

```python
from csvkit_lite import read_csv

for row in read_csv("people.csv"):
    print(row["name"], row["age"])
```

By default, the first line is treated as a header, and each row is returned as a dictionary.

## Automatic type conversion

Enable type inference to convert numbers and booleans automatically:

```python
rows = list(read_csv("people.csv", infer_types=True))
print(rows[0]["age"] + 1)   # 35, since age is an int
```

## Custom delimiters and headers

Use the `delimiter` option for tab-separated or semicolon-separated files. If your file has no header row, supply column names yourself:

```python
rows = read_csv(
    "data.tsv",
    delimiter="\t",
    header=False,
    columns=["id", "score", "label"],
)
```

## Streaming large files

`read_csv` returns a generator, so rows are read lazily and memory usage stays low even for large files:

```python
total = 0
for row in read_csv("huge.csv", infer_types=True):
    total += row["amount"]
print(total)
```

## Loading everything at once

If you prefer a simple list, wrap the call:

```python
data = list(read_csv("people.csv"))
```

## Handling Errors

Malformed rows raise a `CSVParseError` that includes the line number:

```python
from csvkit_lite import read_csv, CSVParseError

try:
    rows = list(read_csv("broken.csv"))
except CSVParseError as err:
    print(f"Problem on line {err.line}: {err}")
```

Pass `skip_errors=True` to ignore bad rows instead.

## Next Steps

- Run the tests with `pytest`
- Read the full API reference in the `docs/` folder
- Report bugs on the GitHub issue tracker

Some redditors seem to think VA panels are just bad. I don't know where that idea comes from, but I disagree with it.

A VA (Vertical Alignment) panel is an LCD that aligns its liquid crystals vertically instead of horizontally, the way traditional LCDs do. That gives it high contrast ratios and deep blacks, which is why gamers and graphic designers like it.

The case against VA usually comes down to three complaints.

1. Viewing angle. Colors and contrast shift if you aren't looking at the panel head-on. That's true, but it only matters if the panel is poorly calibrated or you sit at an extreme angle. Most people sit right in front of their monitors, so for the vast majority of users it's a non-problem.
2. Response time. VA panels are slower than other technologies like TN (Twisted Nematic), which is also true. If you're a hardcore gamer who depends on lightning-fast reflexes, a slower panel might be a problem. Everyone else gets better contrast and color accuracy in exchange, and that's a fair trade.
3. Color accuracy. Some people say VA panels are poor here, and that's not the case. They're known for excellent color accuracy, especially in darker ranges.

1. Viewing angle. A common complaint is that colors and contrast shift if you aren't looking at the panel head-on. However, this is a common misconception. VA panels can have limited viewing angles, but that only matters if the panel is poorly calibrated or you sit at an extreme angle. Most people sit directly in front of their monitors, so for the vast majority of users it's a non-problem.

Italy beat Ireland 17-28 in their Six Nations match at the Stadio Olimpico in Rome.

The Azzurri forwards won the early exchanges against the Irish pack. Number eight Sergio Parisse led the home attack, making several runs and offloading to his support runners.

Ireland's backline found no cohesion against Italy's defence, and the visitors leaned on fly-half Johnny Sexton's boot. He kicked two penalties to keep them in touch.

Winger Luca Sperandio scored Italy's first try in the corner on the half-hour, finishing a sweeping move. Sexton answered with another penalty. Flanker Jake Polledri then crashed over from close range, and Italy led 14-6 at the break.

Amelia Jones is an art historian and theorist who works in art history, art theory, and visual culture. She writes mainly on feminist art history and queer theory.

Early life and education

Jones was born in 1965 in Springfield, Illinois. She studied art history at Yale University and received her undergraduate degree in 1987. She completed a Ph.D. in Visual and Cultural Studies at the University of Rochester in 1992.

Career

Jones taught visual culture at the University of Manchester from 1998 to 2007. She then moved to the University of Southern California, where she is the Robert A. Day Professor of Art & Design and Vice Dean of Critical Studies.

Her work crosses disciplines and covers feminist art, body art, performance art, and film. She draws on both contemporary and historical material, and she often questions conventional readings of it.

Books and lectures

Jones has written and edited several books. They include *Body Art: Performing the Subject* and *Seeing Differently: A History and Theory of Identification in the Visual Arts*. She also edited *The Feminism and Visual Culture Reader*. Her articles have appeared in scholarly journals, and she has lectured internationally, including at the Tate Modern and the Museum of Modern Art.

Ideas

Jones applies feminist and queer theory to historical and contemporary art. She argues for "seeing differently": art has to be understood in the context of the viewer's identity, and aesthetics cannot be separated from social and political concerns.

Influence

Jones has written about underrepresented artists and art forms, and her work has shaped discussion of feminist and queer art within art history.

Judicial murder is the unjust execution of a person through a misused court process, often for political reasons. The proceedings may follow legal procedure on paper, but the outcome falls far short of justice, usually because the judicial system is corrupt or biased.

The idea rests on wrongful execution, which violates the right to life. Related terms include miscarriage of justice, legal homicide, and state-sanctioned murder.

The term describes a paradox. A state's judiciary is supposed to protect the lives and rights of its citizens. In a judicial murder, the court instead takes part in an unlawful killing.

These cases are not new. They go back to antiquity and occur in many cultures and countries. Examples include the execution of Socrates in ancient Greece, the execution of Jesus, which some legal historians regard as a judicial murder, and the execution of Marie-Antoinette during the French Revolution.

In recent history, the best-known cases have mostly been political. When authoritarian regimes execute dissidents after manipulated trials, the cases fit the description.

Contemporary cases draw international condemnation and heavy media attention, especially when the person executed is a prominent political figure.

Judicial murder sets law against justice. The execution is legal under the state's own laws but unjust by human rights norms. That conflict feeds a wider debate over capital punishment, wrongful convictions, and bias in judicial systems.

Proposed remedies include an independent and transparent justice system, fair trials, and stricter standards for evidence. Abolishing the death penalty would largely remove the possibility, and many countries have already done so. Judicial murders still occur.
